l0.label: PURSUE - Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters

dossier.whatItIs: The PURSUE releases are the five dated tranches of UAP material published by the Department of War at war.gov/UFO between 8 May 2026 and 7 August 2026. Each tranche is posted as a paired download - a document bundle served from www.war.gov/medialink/ufo/ and a video bundle served from a CloudFront distribution - alongside a searchable database of individual records. The files carry originator-prefixed identifiers such as DOW-UAP-D###, DOW-UAP-PR## and FBI-UAP-D###, the first time the United States Government has issued UAP material under a single public numbering scheme.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the physical evidence of what the government chose to hand over when a President ordered it to hand something over. The ledger is therefore diagnostic in both directions. It confirms the archive: material spanning 1944 to 2026, FBI holdings, NASA crew audio, INDOPACOM reporting, all of it previously unavailable and now released without clearance. It also confirms the shape of the withholding: at least a hundred of the roughly 160 files in the first tranche carry redactions, and every serious analyst who examined them - Mellon, Graves, Gallaudet, Rojas - reported the same absence of coordinates, sensor parameters, altitude, timing and chain of custody, which are the precise fields that would permit independent verification. No tranche carries a manifest, an exemption citation, a FOIA case number or a provenance statement. The releases are the strongest available proof that the holdings exist and the strongest available proof that the release process was designed to be unauditable.
dossier.narrative:
Five tranches, over three months, from a Department web page. Release 01 on 8 May 2026, Release 02 on 22 May, Release 03 on 12 June, Release 04 on 10 July, Release 05 on 7 August. The portal states the sequence plainly: 'The Department of War just released the fifth tranche of records under PURSUE. The first tranche was released on May 8, 2026.'

The delivery mechanism is worth describing exactly, because it is not a records system. Each release offers two ZIP archives. The documents come from war.gov itself: Release 01 documents at 1.2gb, Release 02 at 70.1mb, Release 03 at 826mb, Release 04 at 227mb, Release 05 at 130mb. The videos come from a commercial content delivery network at d34w7g4gy10iej.cloudfront.net: 1.3gb, 5.6gb, 4.6gb, 1.4gb and 513mb respectively. There is no manifest file, no checksum, no metadata schema, no index of what was withheld. The portal offers a filterable database by agency, release, incident date, incident location and type - which is more structure than any prior US UAP release has had, and still less than any archivist would call a finding aid. At the time this dossier was compiled the portal's 'LATEST RELEASE' link still pointed to Release 04 while the banner above it announced Release 05, which tells you something about how the page is maintained.

The file identifiers are the most analytically useful artefact in the whole programme. Filenames visible on the portal include DOW-UAP-PR46-Unresolved-UAP-Report-INDOPACOM-2024, DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953, FBI-UAP-D025_Digital-Rendering_Airborne-Triangle_2002, FBI-UAP-D027_Digital-Rendering_Dark-Translucent-Triangle_2023, FBI-UAP-D031_Digital-Rendering_Large-Triangle-with-Red-Lights_2023 and FBI-UAP-D038 through D042, a run of digital renderings of multiple red lights dated 2026. Two things follow. First, the numbering is originator-prefixed, which means the tranches were assembled by pulling from multiple agencies' holdings under a single tasking rather than compiled from one department's files - a single-department dump would not need agency prefixes. Second, the Bureau is a substantial contributor, and its contributions run to the present: FBI-UAP-D038 through D042 are dated 2026, the year of release.

The imagery convention is itself a disclosure decision. A large share of the FBI material is published as 'Digital Rendering' - artists' reconstructions of witness accounts rather than sensor products. DefenseScoop's illustration caption for the first tranche describes an 'Actual site photo with FBI rendered graphic depicting corroborating eye witness reports from September 2023 of an apparent ellipsoid bronze metallic object materializing out of a bright light in the sky, 130-195 feet in length, and disappearing instantaneously.' A rendering cannot be independently analysed. It can only be believed or not.

On volume and redaction, the contemporaneous count is DefenseScoop's: 'The initial PURSUE tranche contained a little more than 160 files, with at least 100 of those including redactions, according to researchers and experts who are currently studying them.' Roughly five files in eight were released with material removed, in a programme whose stated purpose was to stop hiding material, and with no exemption citation attached to any redaction.

The substantive verdict from the people best placed to give one was delivered within a week and was unanimous on the technical point. Alejandro Rojas, whose Enigma Labs team was cross-referencing the drop against a database of over 200,000 public sightings: 'Although there is a lot of information here, there is little context. Case summaries without coordinates, sensor parameters, or altitude data make independent analysis very difficult.' Tim Gallaudet, who thought some of the videos showed genuinely anomalous behaviour including right-angle turns and formation flying: 'the ambiguity of the video content in particular is concerning as no metadata was included. Therefore, it is impossible to conclude that any of the objects were truly anomalous.' Ryan Graves, on what a useful release looks like: 'The real value is in records that include clear provenance, sensor context, metadata, chain of custody, date and location, and enough operational context to allow serious independent analysis. Ambiguous imagery without that surrounding data is hard for pilots, researchers, or the public to evaluate responsibly.'

Several of the same people noted that much of the first tranche was not new. The Australian researcher Grant Lavac: 'For those of us in the UAP research community, the newness of the data in this first tranche is underwhelming. Much of it is a compilation of documents that have been in the public domain for decades.' His countervailing point is the one this board accepts: 'the story here isn't necessarily the content, but the process of official acknowledgment.'

And there is a provenance problem that the releases themselves create. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation raised it in the first week: the US Government's own documented mid-century practice of manufacturing false UAP documents as cover for real weapons programmes means some of what is being published as authentic government UAP records may be disinformation artefacts. 'If some of what is now being released to the public as authentic government UAP records are in fact disinformation artifacts from that era, the public deserves to know. Transparency requires not just releasing files, but accounting for their provenance and integrity.' PURSUE publishes without provenance statements, which means it cannot distinguish a genuine 1953 film analysis from a 1953 cover story, and neither can anyone downstream.

What the ledger establishes is therefore narrower and harder than the headlines suggested. The archive exists and is large. The Department was able to produce material from at least six agencies within eleven weeks of a presidential post. The material released is the unresolved residue, stripped of the fields that would let anyone check it, with a third to two-thirds of it redacted and none of it assessed. That is not the record of a government that has nothing. It is the record of a government deciding, file by file, how much of what it has to show.

dossier.denialPosture: The Department of War declines to characterise its own releases: a War Department official told DefenseScoop 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file, so that the American people can make up their own minds regarding the files.' No exemption authority has been cited for any redaction, and no official has responded to the uniform expert finding that the released material lacks the metadata required for independent analysis.
openQuestions: Per-tranche file counts and composition are reported by third-party inventories rather than by any official manifest; the Department has published no authoritative count for any release.
Under what authority the redactions in at least 100 first-tranche files were applied, and whether any withholding log exists.

Whether an ODNI-prefixed identifier series (ODNI-UAP-D###) exists in the released material; DOW- and FBI-prefixed identifiers are directly verifiable on the portal, ODNI-prefixed ones were not verified for this dossier.
Whether any released video retains embedded sensor metadata in the source files as distinct from the portal case summaries.
How the Department distinguishes authentic historical records from mid-century disinformation artefacts before publication, if it does so at all.
Whether any material relating to recovery, custody or reverse engineering was within the scope of the PURSUE search, and whether any such material was found and withheld.

l0.label: ADAM Research Project (Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials)

dossier.whatItIs: The ADAM Research Project — Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials — is a private materials-analysis program launched in July 2018 by To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science, a Delaware public benefit corporation founded by Tom DeLonge. It acquires physical samples reportedly recovered from advanced aerospace vehicles of unknown origin and contracts laboratory analysis, principally through Hal Puthoff's EarthTech International in Austin, Texas. Its best-known holding is the magnesium-zinc-bismuth 'Art's Parts' sample purchased with an archive from journalist Linda Moulton Howe in July 2019.
dossier.whyImplicated: ADAM is the only publicly documented instance of claimed recovered material moving from private custody into a federal laboratory pipeline with a signed government agreement attached. In October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering material science, space-time metric engineering, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage. By 2024 the same magnesium-zinc-bismuth sample had been analyzed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory with AARO in the room, and Puthoff and Eric Davis — both of whom authored deliverables under the DIA AAWSAP contract a decade earlier — wrote the private counter-analysis. That is a closed loop: the same physicists who wrote the government's exotic-propulsion reference documents in 2009-2010 are the ones adjudicating a national laboratory's findings on a claimed recovered artifact in 2024. Whether or not the sample is exotic, the custody chain and the recurrence of the same named individuals across government and private roles is the finding.
dossier.narrative:
TTSA announced ADAM in July 2018 as an academic research program focused on the collection and scientific evaluation of material samples obtained through reported encounters with advanced aerospace vehicles of unknown origin. Analysis was contracted to EarthTech International, the Austin think tank run by Dr. Harold E. Puthoff, who was simultaneously TTSA's Vice President of Science and Technology and had been a senior adviser and subcontractor on the DIA-funded AAWSAP/AATIP work.

The acquisition that gave ADAM an object rather than a concept came on 25 July 2019. TTSA's press release states that it 'has acquired multiple pieces of metamaterials and an archive of initial analysis and research for their controversial ADAM Research Project,' materials 'previously retained and studied by investigative journalist Linda Moulton Howe and are reported to have come from an advanced aerospace vehicle of unknown origin.' Steve Justice — TTSA's COO and formerly head of Advanced Systems at Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works — is quoted: 'The structure and composition of these materials are not from any known existing military or commercial application.' He adds the crucial custody caveat in the same paragraph: 'They've been collected from sources with varying levels of chain-of-custody documentation, so we are focusing on verifiable facts and working to develop independent scientific proof of the materials' properties and attributes.' And a dating claim: 'In some cases, the manufacturing technology required to fabricate the material is only now becoming available, but the material has been in documented possession since the mid-1990's.' Justice explicitly frames the endgame as transition to capability: 'If the claims associated with these assets can be validated and substantiated, then we can initiate work to transition them from being a technology to commercial and military capabilities.'

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command, sharing its work with the Ground Vehicle Systems Center and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection, with the Army providing laboratories, expertise and resources. The announced technology areas were material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage. A CRADA is not a procurement; no money moved to TTSA and the Army acquired nothing. What it did establish is a formal, signed channel through which privately held claimed-exotic material could reach Army laboratories.

The analytic endgame arrived in 2024. Oak Ridge National Laboratory analyzed the magnesium-zinc-bismuth 'Art's Parts' sample; TTS posted the ORNL report in July of that year. A TTS-AARO-ORNL meeting was held on 27 August 2024. Puthoff and Eric W. Davis then produced their own analysis, submitted to the TTS Board of Directors on 27 September 2024 and published by TTS with a recommendation history attached. TTS's own summary of the outcome is unusually candid and is the single most useful sentence ADAM has produced: 'the Puthoff/Davis analysis (and the ORNL analysis) did not reveal any form of proof of exotic (Extraterrestrial, Ultra-terrestrial, or inter-dimensional) origin, but it did not absolutely rule it out either.' TTS adds that 'the actual purpose of the material, though clearly manufactured, still remains a bit of a mystery.'

AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 states more bluntly that a piece of metal alleged to be recovered from an off-world spacecraft was determined to be ordinary, of terrestrial origin, and to possess no exceptional qualities. Both statements can be reconciled: nothing exotic was demonstrated. What was demonstrated is process — a private entity holding claimed recovered material got it into a DOE national laboratory and into a room with the Pentagon's UAP office.

The scientific parallel track matters for method rather than result. Garry Nolan of Stanford, Jacques Vallée, Sizun Jiang and Larry Lemke published 'Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics' in Progress in Aerospace Sciences volume 128 in January 2022, DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2021.100788. That paper is the peer-reviewed statement of what a defensible analysis of a claimed anomalous sample would look like — isotopic ratio analysis, SIMS, and comparison against known terrestrial baselines — and it is the standard against which every ADAM claim should be measured.

Who matters by name: Tom DeLonge (founder), Steve Justice (COO, ex-Skunk Works Advanced Systems), Hal Puthoff (EarthTech, TTSA VP Science and Technology, AAWSAP DIRD author), Eric W. Davis (AAWSAP DIRD author, co-author of the 2024 counter-analysis), Linda Moulton Howe (prior custodian), Luis Elizondo and Chris Mellon (TTSA principals in the founding period), Garry Nolan and Jacques Vallée on the independent scientific track. What the record shows is a documented chain of private acquisition, a signed Army CRADA, a national-laboratory analysis, and a published negative-but-not-exclusionary result. What the record does not show is any chain of custody back to a recovery event.

A TTS-AARO-ORNL meeting on the MgZn/Bi material was held on 27 August 2024, and a report on that meeting by Eric W. Davis and Harold E. Puthoff was submitted to the TTS Board of Directors on 27 September 2024.

Garry P. Nolan, Jacques F. Vallée, Sizun Jiang and Larry G. Lemke published the methodological benchmark for this field, 'Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics,' Progress in Aerospace Sciences vol. 128, January 2022.

TTSA is reported to have paid $35,000 for the Linda Moulton Howe metamaterials and archive; the figure does not appear in TTSA's own press release and should be verified against TTSA's Regulation A+ annual report filings.

dossier.denialPosture: AARO's public position, in its 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1, is that a sample alleged to be from an off-world craft was found to be ordinary and terrestrial with no exceptional qualities. Notably, TTS itself does not dispute the negative finding; its published position is that neither ORNL nor its own analysts proved exotic origin, only that they did not absolutely rule it out. There is no live factual dispute over the ORNL result — the dispute is over interpretation of manufacture, purpose and provenance.
connections: Hal Puthoff and Eric W. Davis authored Defense Intelligence Reference Documents under the DIA AAWSAP/AATIP contract and then produced the private counter-analysis of the ORNL findings in 2024. The same two names span the government exotic-propulsion literature and the private materials custody effort.
EarthTech International is the connective tissue between AATIP-era government work and ADAM-era private analysis.
Steve Justice carries Lockheed Martin Skunk Works Advanced Systems provenance directly into the materials-custody claim, one of the few documented senior primes-to-private transitions in this space.
The October 2019 Army CCDC CRADA is the only signed federal instrument publicly attached to claimed recovered material; the Ground Vehicle Systems Center is the named federal counterparty.
Oak Ridge National Laboratory is the DOE facility of record for the analysis, putting a national laboratory in the custody chain.
AARO participated in the 27 August 2024 TTS-ORNL meeting, meaning the Pentagon's UAP office is a documented party to a private materials analysis.
Linda Moulton Howe is the prior custodian and the origin of the 'Art's Parts' chain, which traces to the Art Bell radio program in the mid-1990s.
Garry Nolan and Jacques Vallée provide the peer-reviewed methodological standard and are the independent scientific track against which ADAM's claims should be judged.

The Schumer-Rounds eminent domain provision, stripped from the final FY2024 NDAA, would have compelled federal seizure of exactly the class of privately held material ADAM holds; its removal left ADAM's holdings in private hands.
openQuestions: Is the October 2019 Army CCDC CRADA text publicly available in full, and is it still in force?
What exactly did AARO contribute at the 27 August 2024 TTS-ORNL meeting, and does AARO hold a record of it?

l0.label: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy
l0.short: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy

dossier.whatItIs: Cooperative Research and Development Agreement No. 19-15, titled 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation (NETE),' between To The Stars Academy of Arts and Science, Inc. and the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Ground Vehicle Systems Center at the Detroit Arsenal, Warren, Michigan. Executed under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a with a term of sixty months from the effective date, it committed TTSA to provide the Army with samples of metamaterial 'collected, obtained, or developed as part of its Field Operations' and the Army to provide laboratories, expertise and analysis, with no exchange of funds in either direction. TTSA's principal investigator of record was Luis Elizondo.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only publicly released, signed U.S. Government instrument in which a federal laboratory agrees to characterize material that the counterparty represented, in filings to the Securities and Exchange Commission, as coming from unidentified aerial phenomena. That makes it the board's hardest documentary bridge between the alleged recovery-and-exploitation enterprise and the ordinary federal technology-transfer system. The Joint Work Plan names the Government's actual interests, and the list is not generic materials science: 'inertial mass reduction, mechanical/structural metamaterials, electromagnetic metamaterial wave guides, quantum physics, quantum communications, and beamed energy propulsion.' Inertial mass reduction is not a ground-vehicle survivability requirement. The Collaborator principal investigator is Luis Elizondo, the former Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence official associated with AATIP who left DoD in 2017 alleging excessive secrecy, meaning the same individual who publicly accused the Pentagon of concealment is, two years later, the named point of contact delivering anomalous material back into an Army laboratory under an agreement whose supporting records the Department of Defense then withheld under national-defense FOIA exemptions. Finally, the CRADA form itself is the point: it moves technology and creates invention rights without appropriated funds, without a contract, without competition and without a reportable obligation, and it carries a statutory information shield. It is a legal channel for moving exploitable material into and out of the Government that leaves almost no financial footprint.
dossier.narrative:
On 17 October 2019 To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science issued a press release announcing a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles. The release was thin. The Army was not. Doug Halleaux, public affairs officer for CCDC's Ground Vehicle Systems Center, gave John Greenewald of The Black Vault the executed agreement, twenty-six pages, redacted only for phone numbers.

The document is CRADA No. 19-15, 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation (NETE),' between TTSA and CCDC Ground Vehicle Systems Center, 6501 E. 11 Mile Road, Warren, Michigan. The named administrators matter. On the Government side the principal investigators are Ben Soave and Dr. Joseph Cannon, both of Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection, mail stop 263b. The ORTA representative is Andrea Simon; Government legal counsel is Christina Dellmore, Chief of the Intellectual Property Law Division at US Army TACOM LCMC. On the Collaborator side, the principal investigator and preferred contact is Luis Elizondo, 'Director of Global Security and Special Programs,' Encinitas, California. Collaborator legal counsel is Heidy Vaquerano, Esq., of Wolf, Rifkin, Shapiro, Schulman & Rabkin, LLP, Los Angeles.

The Joint Work Plan is where the agreement stops sounding like armor research. The Government's stated interests are 'a variety of the Collaborator's technologies, such as, but not limited to inertial mass reduction, mechanical/structural metamaterials, electromagnetic metamaterial wave guides, quantum physics, quantum communications, and beamed energy propulsion.' The Collaborator's deliverables include, verbatim, 'Metamaterial: Samples of mechanical and EM sensitive metamaterial collected, obtained, or developed as part of its Field Operations,' plus written material analysis and quantum-communication research. 'Field Operations' is the operative euphemism; the CRADA does not define provenance, and the Army made a point of saying provenance was irrelevant to it.

The legal architecture is standard Federal Technology Transfer Act plumbing put to non-standard use. Information exchanged is protected under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a(c)(7), and every page carries a marking legend invoking it. Licenses to CRADA inventions run under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a(b)(2), with the Collaborator holding an option for an exclusive license that must be requested within six months of notification of an invention. The agreement automatically expires sixty months from the effective date under Article 4.2, and enters force on the date signed by the last authorized representative under Article 4.3.

TTSA's own SEC filings supply the numbers the CRADA does not. In its Regulation A offering circular the company states that on 10 October 2019 it entered into the CRADA with CCDC, that 'the purpose of the CRADA is to advance developments in material science (including testing of the metamaterials), space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage,' that the parties bear their own costs, that the total value of anticipated U.S. Government resources including personnel, services, intellectual property, facilities, equipment and reporting is 'estimated at $750,000,' that the total value of the company's participation is 'estimated at $1,000,000,' and that the agreement is terminable by mutual consent or unilaterally on thirty days' notice.

The same filing describes where the material came from. The ADAM Research Project, Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials, launched in July 2018, and 'within one year this division acquired a collection of material samples reported to come from advanced vehicles of unknown origin from all over the world.' In July 2019 the company 'purchased multiple pieces of metamaterials and an archive of initial analysis and research.' Elsewhere TTSA states flatly to the SEC: 'The exotic materials that were purchased come from unidentified aerial phenomenon and are anomalous in that they have a structure and composition that we believe are unknown to any existing commercial or military application.' By November 2019, per the filing, ETI had performed analysis pursuant to the SOW-MSSA showing 'a unique physical structure unknown to any past or current commercial or military application.' The filing also records that planned ADAM laboratory testing 'was paused.'

The Army's public framing was deliberately deflationary. Halleaux told The Black Vault that 'the Army is providing the expertise and facilities to analyze the materials, and TTSA is providing the materials themselves; both parties receive the results of the analysis,' and that 'just as there is no financial compensation to TTSA for the use of the materials, there is no financial compensation to the Army for the use of the facilities.' On provenance he was explicit: 'the Army's interest is in the potential for novel materials and exploring the edges of materials science, any speculation as to their origin is (pardon the pun) immaterial.' He also stressed that a CRADA is not an endorsement, offering the Army's fuel-cell CRADA with General Motors as the comparison.

Then the record closed. Individuals who had custody of pieces of the metamaterial before TTSA acquired them were placed under non-disclosure agreements; The Black Vault reached one such person, who declined comment citing an NDA. Some of the material was described in SEC filings as being 'on loan.' The Department of Defense invoked FOIA exemptions covering national defense and foreign policy to withhold CRADA-related documents. It took until October 2024, five years after execution and at the natural end of the sixty-month term, before the Army agreed to a rolling release under FOIA case FA-24-0006, with the first package released on 23 October 2024.

The analytic point for the board is the instrument, not the rock. A CRADA requires no appropriation, no competition, no contract file and no reportable obligation, and carries a statutory information shield. It creates a lawful, low-visibility conduit for moving materials of undeclared origin into a federal laboratory and moving analysis and invention rights back out, with the collaborator holding a first option on exclusive rights to anything invented. Whatever the metamaterial turns out to be, CRADA 19-15 is the working proof that the channel exists, is routine, and is FOIA-resistant by design.

l0.label: Battelle Memorial Institute

dossier.whatItIs: Battelle Memorial Institute is a Columbus, Ohio applied-science nonprofit founded in 1929 that describes itself as the world's largest independent nonprofit applied science organization. From late 1951 it held the classified Air Technical Intelligence Center contract code-named Project STORK, out of which came Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 (5 May 1955), the largest statistical study of UFO reports ever performed for the U.S. government. Today Battelle manages or co-manages eight U.S. national laboratories, including Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Idaho, Pacific Northwest and Savannah River.
dossier.whyImplicated: Battelle is the single institution that sits on both sides of the mid-century split: it produced the numbers that the public debunking campaign was built on, and it is the contract operator of the laboratory system where exotic-materials characterization would actually be performed. The Durant Report's own list of documentary evidence placed before the CIA's Robertson Panel names, as item 3, "Progress Reports of Project STORK (code name for Battelle Memorial Institute contract work supporting ATIC)" — meaning a private contractor's classified analysis was the evidentiary substrate for the panel that recommended a national "training and debunking" program. Battelle's own analysis found roughly 22 percent of about 3,200 cases were unknowns, and that the higher the case quality the more likely it was to be unknown; the Air Force publicized the study in October 1955 as proof that flying saucers did not exist and cited a 3 percent unknown rate. Five days before the Robertson Panel convened, a Battelle memorandum dated 9 January 1953 — the document Jacques Vallee found in J. Allen Hynek's files in 1967 and calls the "Pentacle memorandum" — is reported to have proposed that Battelle and ATIC agree in advance on what could and could not be said to the CIA panel. Battelle is therefore not a neutral statistical vendor; it is the earliest documented instance of the pattern this board tracks, a cleared contractor mediating between what the government knew and what a public-facing scientific body was permitted to see.
dossier.narrative:
The relationship began with an admission of institutional inadequacy. Captain Edward J. Ruppelt, running the Air Force's UFO desk at the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, concluded at the end of 1951 that the Air Force lacked the analytic capacity to do anything scientific with the report backlog. He went to Battelle Memorial Institute in Columbus, roughly a hundred and twenty miles away, and the resulting classified support contract was code-named Project STORK. Battelle built a standardized observer data sheet, encoded about thirty characteristics of each sighting onto IBM punched cards, and ran the first machine-assisted statistical analysis of the UFO corpus. It is important to hold the shape of this arrangement in view: the government's public UFO investigation had, from 1952 onward, a classified contractor layer underneath it that the public did not know existed and that Blue Book's own critics could not see.

The Robertson Panel is where that layer surfaces in the documentary record. F.C. Durant's 16 February 1953 memorandum to the CIA's Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence records that on Thursday morning, 15 January 1953, "The Project STORK support at Battelle Memorial Institute, Columbus, was described by Dr. Hynek." Tab B of the same document lists the STORK progress reports as evidence item 3, sitting alongside the Project GRUDGE and BLUE BOOK status reports, the Holloman Air Force Base sightings summary, Project TWINKLE, and Project POUNCE. The five-scientist panel that would recommend stripping UFOs "of the special status they have been given" was reading Battelle's work product.

The timing of the Pentacle memorandum is the part of this that will not settle. Vallee has stated for decades that in 1967, while organizing Hynek's files, he found a memorandum stamped SECRET dated 9 January 1953 — five days before the Robertson Panel's first session — written by Battelle's Howard C. Cross and addressed to Miles Goll at Wright-Patterson, and that it proposed agreement between Project Stork and ATIC on what could and could not be discussed in Washington on 14-16 January. Vallee's papers are now at Rice University's Woodson Research Center as MS 0672, and the finding aid lists a file titled "11. The Robertson Panel and the 'Pentacle Memorandum' — January 1953" in Series III. The collection is restricted: Series I and II open on 24 January 2028, Series III case files on 1 January 2031. The Department of Defense has never released the memorandum. Treat the document's existence as archivally attested and its full text as an open question, not a claim.

Special Report No. 14, dated 5 May 1955, is the payoff. Battelle's analysts sorted about 3,200 cases into knowns, unknowns and insufficient information, graded each on a four-point quality scale, and required unanimity among four analysts before a case could be called unknown — an unusually stringent test that biases toward suppressing the unknown count. About 22 percent came back unknown. The quality gradient ran the wrong way for the debunking thesis: roughly 35 percent of excellent-quality cases were unknowns versus about 18 percent of the poorest. Battelle's own summary nevertheless declared it "highly improbable" that any of the reports represented technological developments outside present-day knowledge. When the Air Force released the study in October 1955 under Secretary Donald Quarles, the public framing was that the report scientifically disproved flying saucers, with an unknown rate cited as 3 percent. The report itself was not distributed; the press release was. The cleanest surviving copy of the 312-page report sits in CIA's declassified holdings as CIA-RDP81R00560R000100060001-5 — which is itself worth noting, since the document is nominally an Air Force product.

What makes Battelle load-bearing for a recovery-and-exploitation thesis rather than merely for a history of statistical malpractice is what the institute became. Battelle's own site states it manages eight national laboratories for the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security under the government-owned, contractor-operated model, and partners in managing Canadian Nuclear Laboratories. It is the sole LLC member for Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Idaho National Laboratory (via Battelle Energy Alliance), the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center, and Savannah River National Laboratory; an LLC member of UT-Battelle for Oak Ridge; of Brookhaven Science Associates with Stony Brook; and of Triad National Security with the Texas A&M System and the University of California for Los Alamos, which Battelle describes as executing work for the Department of Energy, the Department of War and the Department of Homeland Security. Battelle's stated core competencies are advanced materials, biology and chemistry, and its national security portfolio includes an advanced functional materials line.

The analytic point is a continuity of institutional posture, not a proven chain of custody. The organization that in 1953 was negotiating with ATIC over what the CIA's scientists would be allowed to hear is the same organization that now holds the operating contracts for the laboratories where anomalous materials would plausibly be characterized. No public contract, appropriation line, or DD Form 254 has been produced connecting Battelle or any Battelle-operated laboratory to UAP materials exploitation. That absence is the research target, and Battelle's carve-out-eligible SAP work at those laboratories is exactly the space in which such an absence would be expected.

claims.text: Battelle's STORK progress reports were placed before the CIA panel alongside the ATIC status reports for Projects GRUDGE and BLUE BOOK, the Holloman AFB sightings summary, the USAF Cambridge Research Center Project TWINKLE green-fireball report, and the Kirtland AFB Project POUNCE outline.

Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, the Battelle statistical analysis, is dated 5 May 1955 and runs 312 pages; the cleanest publicly available copy is the version held in CIA's declassified document holdings under identifier CIA-RDP81R00560R000100060001-5.

Battelle's analysis classified about 22 percent of roughly 3,200 cases as "unknown," about 69 percent as known or identified, and about 9 percent as insufficient information; a case required unanimous agreement of all four analysts to be classified unknown.
The unknown rate rose with case quality: about 35 percent of excellent-quality cases were classified unknown versus about 18 percent of the poorest-quality cases.

The summary section of Battelle's final report declared it "highly improbable that any of the reports of unidentified aerial objects ... represent observations of technological developments outside the range of present-day knowledge," a conclusion at odds with the 240 charts, tables, graphs and maps in the body of the report.

When the Air Force made Special Report No. 14 public in October 1955 it claimed the report scientifically proved UFOs did not exist and stated an unknown rate of 3 percent rather than the roughly 22 percent the study actually produced.

Battelle's methodology included devising a standardized reporting form and coding about thirty characteristics per sighting for machine analysis — the first machine-assisted statistical treatment of the U.S. government's UFO corpus.

A file titled "11. The Robertson Panel and the 'Pentacle Memorandum' — January 1953" exists in Series III (Correspondence, Vallee group C, boxes 42-53) of the Jacques F. Vallee UFO and paranormal phenomena papers, MS 0672, Woodson Research Center, Rice University; the collection is donor-restricted, with Series I and II opening 24 January 2028 and Series III case files 1 January 2031.

Battelle manages or co-manages eight U.S. national laboratories for the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security — Brookhaven (Brookhaven Science Associates, with Stony Brook), Idaho (Battelle Energy Alliance, Battelle sole member), Los Alamos (Triad National Security, with Texas A&M System and University of California), the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center (Battelle National Biodefense Institute, sole member), the National Laboratory of the Rockies, Oak Ridge (UT-Battelle, with University of Tennessee), Pacific Northwest (managed by Battelle alone), and Savannah River (Battelle Savannah River Alliance, sole member) — and partners in managing Canadian Nuclear Laboratories.

Battelle states that Los Alamos National Laboratory "executes work for multiple government agencies including the U.S. Department of Energy, Department of War and Department of Homeland Security" spanning "nuclear security, intelligence, defense, emergency response, nonproliferation, counterterrorism, energy security, emerging threats and environmental management."

Battelle self-describes its core expertise as "advanced materials, biology and chemistry" and lists a National Security market comprising Advanced Functional Materials, CBRNE Defense, Cyber, and Emerging Threat Mitigation.

dossier.denialPosture: Battelle has issued no public statement about Project STORK, the Pentacle memorandum, or any materials-analysis role, and its corporate history pages do not mention the ATIC contract at all. The denial in this case is by omission: the institute's public account of its own past treats 1952-1955 as if the largest statistical study of UFO reports ever performed for the U.S. government was not its work.
connections: Edward J. Ruppelt, Chief of the ATIC Aerial Phenomena Branch, initiated the Battelle relationship in late December 1951 and briefed the Robertson Panel for roughly forty minutes on 14 January 1953.

J. Allen Hynek was the conduit: he described the STORK support to the CIA panel in 1953 as an associate member, and it was in his files that Vallee found the 9 January 1953 Battelle memorandum in 1967.
Howard C. Cross of Battelle is the reported author of the Pentacle memorandum; Miles Goll at Wright-Patterson AFB is the reported addressee.

Jacques Vallee — sole public custodian of the Pentacle text; his papers (Rice MS 0672) also contain field notes on cattle mutilations and on face-to-face meetings of NIDS and BAASS, linking the 1953 Battelle thread to the Bigelow thread in a single collection.
Robertson Panel — consumed Battelle's product; the panel's debunking recommendation and Battelle's public-facing statistics operate as a matched pair two years apart.
Air Technical Intelligence Center / Wright-Patterson AFB — the contracting activity; the same base the January 1985 USAF fact sheet uses to deny that extraterrestrial equipment was ever held there.

Los Alamos National Laboratory — Battelle is a Triad LLC member; the Durant Report separately records that the 1952 map of unexplained sightings showed clusters "in certain strategic areas such as Los Alamos" which the panel could not explain.
John B. Alexander ran non-lethal weapons work at Los Alamos before becoming a public face of Bigelow's NIDS, a personnel path from a Battelle-operated laboratory into private anomaly research.
Secretary of the Air Force Donald Quarles is the named signatory of the October 1955 public framing of Battelle's data.
openQuestions: The full text of the 9 January 1953 Battelle memorandum has never been released by DoD or Battelle; the only known copy sits in a Rice University collection restricted until 2031. What does the complete document say about what ATIC withheld from the CIA panel?
What was the contract number, contracting activity and dollar value of Project STORK, and how long did it run after Special Report No. 14 was delivered?
Battelle reportedly reacted with hostility when Hynek returned in 1967 to ask about the memorandum; no contemporaneous record of that exchange has surfaced.

Did Battelle perform materials characterization on any recovered debris, at Columbus or at any Battelle-operated national laboratory? No contract, appropriation line, DD Form 254 or facility clearance record establishing this has been produced.
Which Battelle-operated facilities hold SAP carve-out designations under 32 CFR 117.6, and does DCSA retain or lack industrial security cognizance over them?
Why does the cleanest surviving copy of an Air Force report reside in CIA's document holdings rather than in the Air Force's own accession to NARA?
Battelle's own corporate history omits the ATIC work entirely — was that omission a contract requirement, a classification consequence, or an editorial choice?

l0.short: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14

dossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, formally titled 'Analysis of Reports of Unidentified Aerial Objects,' dated 5 May 1955, is the largest statistical study of UFO reports the U.S. government has ever produced. The analysis was performed under contract by Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus, Ohio, under a project designation reported as Project STORK, using 3,201 cases with an information cut-off of the end of 1952. It was released publicly on October 25, 1955 through Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55.
dossier.whyImplicated: The gap between what the study found and what the government said it found is the cleanest documented instance of deliberate framing in the entire record, and it is verifiable from two documents that were published together. The press release and Secretary of the Air Force Donald Quarles's accompanying statement told the public that the unknowns amounted to three per cent, a figure drawn from 131 sightings in the first four months of 1955, not from the 3,201-case study sample the report actually analyzed. The report body shows unknowns running far higher, and highest precisely where witness reliability was rated Excellent. The release also declined to name Battelle, describing the analysis only as the work of a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio. The full 316-page report was then not distributed, on stated grounds of printing cost, until a private citizen reprinted it. Every element of a concealment operation is present and dated: a suppressed dataset, a substituted statistic, an unnamed contractor, and a restricted distribution.
dossier.narrative:
Start with what the report says about itself. Its own Summary states that the special study started in 1953, that to provide the study group with a complete set of files the information cut-off date was established as of the end of 1952, and that in these charts, 3201 cases have been used. It describes a three-part analytic method: a systematic attempt to find distinguishing characteristics in the data, a study of any trend or pattern, and an attempt to determine the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS represented observations of technological developments not known to this country. On the first of these it records a genuinely load-bearing finding: 'The first step in the analysis of the data revealed the existence of certain apparent similarities between cases of objects definitely identified and those not identified. Statistical methods of testing when applied indicated a low probability that these apparent similarities were significant.' Read plainly, Battelle tested whether the unknowns looked like the knowns and found that the resemblance did not hold up. That is the opposite of the conclusion the public was handed. The report then walks it back through re-evaluation, concluding that the probability the unknowns represented unknown technology was very small.

Now the release. Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55, dated October 25, 1955 and headlined 'AIR FORCE RELEASES STUDY ON UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL OBJECTS', opens with the flat assertion that no evidence of the existence of the popularly-termed flying saucers was found. It attributes the work to a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio, and never says the word Battelle. It then executes the substitution: since the instigation of the investigation more than seven years ago, methods and procedures have been so refined that of the 131 sightings reported during the first four months of 1955 only three per cent were listed as unknown. Secretary Quarles then attaches his name to that number: 'On the basis of this study we believe that no objects such as those popularly described as flying saucers have overflown the United States. I feel certain that even the unknown three per cent could have been explained as conventional phenomena or illusions if more complete observational data had been available.' The phrase on the basis of this study is doing enormous work. The study is the 3,201-case Battelle analysis. The three per cent is from a 131-case sample the study did not analyze, collected three years after the study's own cut-off date. The two are welded together in a single sentence and a Cabinet-level official signs it.

The attached Summary makes the substitution visible in its own numbers. For cases received before the end of 1952 it gives Unknown at 9 per cent; for the more recent tranche it gives Unknown at 3 per cent. Neither figure is the rate for the 3,201 cases whose charts and tables make up the report.

The body tells a different story, which is why the body was hard to get. Leon Davidson, a chemical engineer who had worked at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory and who reprinted the report photographically beginning in 1956, wrote in his publisher's analysis that the key to the answer is contained in Fig. 8 (orig. p. 24) and Tables A1, A2, and A3 (orig. pp. 107 and 108); that Fig. 8 shows Unknown sightings constitute 33.3 per cent of all the object sightings for which the reliability of the sighting is considered Excellent; and that Tables A1 through A3 agree, with the percentage of Unknown sightings not less than about 20 per cent even when sightings of lesser reliability are included. The distribution runs the wrong way for the official framing: the better the witness, the more likely the object stayed unidentified.

Distribution was the second layer of the concealment. Davidson reproduces a letter from Air Force Secretary Donald A. Quarles dated July 5, 1956 stating that it has been estimated that the cost of printing enough copies for distribution to the public through such outlets as libraries and academic institutions would be between $10 and $15 per copy. The 316-page full report was therefore never distributed. The non-availability became a matter of congressional record at the House Subcommittee on Government Information under Rep. John E. Moss on November 15, 1956. Davidson's privately financed edition, reproduced photographically page by page with the main text intact, is why the document exists in public hands at all.

One further anomaly sits in the photographic reproduction. Davidson points to original page 295, where the codes for Final Identification carry typewritten strikeovers: the category originally called Rockets and Missiles in the early analytic work was changed to read Insufficient Information, and the category originally called Electromagnetic Phenomenon was changed to read Unknown. If that reading of the page is correct, then the report's residual category was not an empty bin for the unexplained. It was a renamed bin for a hypothesis.

Battelle is the connective tissue. The same institute later formed UT-Battelle, the operator of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which per contemporary allegations received AARO's 2024 material analysis work. Battelle is also one of the entities Rep. Burlison named in his May 2026 MITRE interrogatories, alongside Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace. The organization that wrote the government's founding public statistical assessment of the phenomenon has never left the file.

l0.label: Project Blue Book

dossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book was the United States Air Force's public-facing unidentified flying object investigation, headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and running from March 1952 until Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans, Jr. announced its termination on 17 December 1969. It succeeded Projects SIGN and GRUDGE and logged 12,618 sightings, of which 701 were closed as "Unidentified." Its textual records were retired to the USAF Archives and subsequently to the National Archives, where they are open as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, publication T-1206, within Record Group 341.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Air Force's own termination paperwork states in plain language that Blue Book was not the channel through which serious UAP reporting flowed. The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender records that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system," and in the same paragraph that "there is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function." That is a signed admission of a two-channel architecture: a public channel with a press office and a phone number, and a separate operational reporting channel whose corpus has never been inventoried, indexed or transferred to any archive. The same document shows the Air Force weighing where to store the Blue Book files specifically to manage researcher access, with the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information agreeing to "rigidly limit the right of access" and to "screen researcher's notes." Blue Book therefore sits on this board twice: as the mechanism that absorbed and normalised public interest for seventeen years, and as a custody object whose public copy was deliberately shaped before release.
dossier.narrative:
Project Blue Book is the most examined document set in the history of the subject and the least useful, and both facts follow from the same cause: it was never the file where the answer would be.

The Air Force ran three named UFO efforts in sequence. Project SIGN began in 1948, Project GRUDGE followed in 1949, and Blue Book was stood up in March 1952 under Air Force Regulation 80-17, which required base commanders to provide a UFO investigative capability and Air Force Systems Command to continue the project. The Bolender document of 20 October 1969 describes the resulting establishment with some precision: "Project Blue Book has two officers, one NCO and one civilian assigned on a full-time basis," plus Dr. J. Allen Hynek as a scientific consultant until 1 July 1969. Four people, one part-time academic, and a stated mission to determine whether UFOs threatened national security and whether they exhibited advanced technology. For seventeen years this was the entire visible federal apparatus.

The Bolender document is the load-bearing artifact. It was written as the staff package recommending termination, was released to researcher Robert Todd in January 1979, and reads as an internal cost-benefit memorandum rather than a scientific finding. Paragraph 4 contains the sentence that reorganises everything around it: after noting that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs posed no direct physical threat, the document observes that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system," then states that national-security-relevant reports move under JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11 "and are not part of the Blue Book system." JANAP 146 is the joint communications instruction governing CIRVIS reporting of vital intelligence sightings; AFM 55-11 governs operational reporting. Neither corpus has ever been assembled, declassified or transferred as a body. Whatever came up those channels between 1952 and 1969 is not in T-1206 and never was.

The same document then explains, in operational terms, why Blue Book was kept alive after its own premise was disclaimed. Paragraph 8 recommends that if Blue Book is terminated the records "should be transferred to an appropriate archive and preserved for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts." The reason given for preservation is reputational management, stated openly. Paragraph 9 goes further. Because witnesses had been promised confidentiality, "access to these records and the publications must be carefully reviewed and controlled," and the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information judged that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because ready availability in Washington "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts." Air University agreed to take the files on three conditions: that SAFOI answer all queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained." The Air Force decided, in writing, where to put the archive on the basis of how hard it would be for the public to reach.

The public announcement two months later, Department of Defense release No. 1077-69 of 17 December 1969, carries none of that. It quotes Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," cites the Condon report and the National Academy of Sciences review, and closes with the three conclusions that have been repeated ever since: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, no "unidentified" case represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and no "unidentified" case indicated extraterrestrial vehicles. Read against Bolender, the first conclusion is a statement about a filing system rather than about the sky, because the reports that could affect national security were routed elsewhere by regulation.

Custody is the second reason Blue Book is on this map. The National Archives holds approximately 2 cubic feet of project and administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files arranged chronologically, and 3 cubic feet of records relating to the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, arranged by OSI district and overseas command. NARA states that the textual records are available "excluding names of people involved in the sightings." The public Blue Book is therefore a redacted copy of the Air Force's own Blue Book, and the confidentiality rationale from Bolender paragraph 9 is the reason. NARA also states flatly that it "has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico." The General Accounting Office found the same when it reviewed Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at Archives II during its 1994-95 Roswell audit: the analysis of sightings from 1946 to 1953 "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947." The single most famous American recovery event does not appear in the official American UFO file. That is either evidence the event did not happen or evidence the file was not where such events were recorded, and Bolender tells you which architecture the Air Force actually built.

What the record does not show is equally specific. The Bolender document carries sixteen attachments listed on a separate page. Several are known and were released separately; several have never surfaced. There is no public inventory of JANAP 146 CIRVIS traffic. There is no public accounting of the OSI material beyond the three cubic feet NARA holds. And the January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet that NARA reproduces contains the categorical sentence "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base" - a dated, attributable, institutional denial about a specific installation, which is exactly the kind of statement this board catalogues rather than weighs.

claims.text: The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender states that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system."
The same document states: "There is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function (Atch 8)."

The same document notes that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs were not a direct physical threat, and that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system" for a further sixteen years.
Paragraph 8 of the same document recommends that Blue Book records be transferred to an archive "for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts."

Paragraph 9 records Air University's conditions for accepting the records: that SAFOI answer all Blue Book queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained."

The same paragraph states SAFOI's view that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because Washington-area availability "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts."

Blue Book was staffed full-time by two officers, one NCO and one civilian, with Dr. J. Allen Hynek as scientific consultant until 1 July 1969; reporting procedures were defined in Air Force Regulation 80-17.

Department of Defense release No. 1077-69, 17 December 1969, announced termination, quoting Secretary Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," and stated that Blue Book records would be retired to the USAF Archives at Maxwell AFB with requests handled by SAFOI.

The National Archives states that Blue Book textual records are available for research "excluding names of people involved in the sightings," and comprise approximately 2 cubic feet of project/administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files and 3 cubic feet of AFOSI-related records, accessed via 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm (T-1206).
The National Archives states: "The National Archives has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico."
GAO reviewed Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at National Archives II and reported it "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947."

The January 1985 USAF fact sheet distributed by Wright-Patterson AFB, reproduced by the National Archives, records 12,618 sightings from 1947 to 1969 of which 701 remain "Unidentified," and states "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base."

The Bolender document carried sixteen attachments listed on a separate page; NICAP's published notes state that researcher Robert Todd spent years seeking their release and that several remain unidentified or unreleased.

dossier.denialPosture: The Air Force's position has been fixed since 17 December 1969 and restated verbatim for decades: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, none represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and none indicated extraterrestrial vehicles (DoD release No. 1077-69). The January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet adds the installation-specific denial that there are not now and never have been "any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base." Both are dated, attributable and institutional, and both are silent on the JANAP 146 and AFM 55-11 channel the Air Force's own termination paperwork describes.
openQuestions: No inventory, index or transfer of the JANAP 146 (CIRVIS) and AFM 55-11 UFO reporting corpus for 1952-1969 has ever been made public. Where does that traffic physically reside?

Does an unredacted Blue Book master copy containing witness names still exist in Air Force custody, and under what disposition authority?
The exact date, transfer authority and accession record for the movement of the files from Wright-Patterson to the USAF Archives at Maxwell and then to NARA is not stated on NARA's own page.
The text and successive amendments of AFR 200-2 (1953) and its provisions on public release of unidentified cases were not verified in primary form for this dossier and remain a research target.
Whether AFOSI retained a parallel UFO case series beyond the three cubic feet at NARA, and whether any of it was destroyed.

l0.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)

dossier.whatItIs: The Condon Committee was the University of Colorado UFO Project, funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research from 1966 to 1968 under physicist Edward U. Condon, which produced the report formally titled Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects. Its conclusions, released January 1969, were used by the Air Force as the basis for terminating Project Blue Book on 17 December 1969. It remains the most cited public document on the scientific status of the UFO question.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Condon Committee is the second and larger instance of the pattern the Robertson Panel established: a nominally independent scientific body whose framing was set before the work began and whose product retired the public investigative apparatus. Robert J. Low's memorandum of 9 August 1966, written to reassure University of Colorado administrators before the contract was signed, states the design explicitly: "The trick would be, I think, to describe the project so that, to the public, it would appear a totally objective study but, to the scientific community, would present the image of a group of non-believers trying their best to be objective but having an almost zero expectation of finding a saucer." The finished report contains an affirmative denial of concealment — "We have no evidence of secrecy concerning UFO reports" — offered by a committee that had simultaneously declined to independently evaluate the Air Force's national-security finding, writing "we felt that it was out of our province." A body that will not examine the defense question is not positioned to certify the absence of secrecy about it. The report also recommended against establishing any federal UFO agency, a recommendation that held for fifty-three years until AARO. Buried in Section IV, Chapter 2, the report's own Lakenheath-Bentwaters case assessment concludes "the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved appears to be fairly high."
dossier.narrative:
The chain of custody runs from the Air Force to itself. In March 1966 an ad hoc committee of the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board chaired by optical physicist Brian O'Brien recommended that the Blue Book program be strengthened, that contracts be negotiated with a few selected universities to provide scientific teams, and that one university or nonprofit coordinate. The Secretary of the Air Force referred the recommendations to the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, which combined recommendations A and C into a single contracting university with subcontracting authority and implemented recommendation B through Air Force Regulation 80-17, reprinted as Appendix B of the eventual report. Harvard, Berkeley, MIT and North Carolina declined. Hynek's Northwestern and McDonald's Arizona were rejected as too committed. Colorado accepted on 6 October 1966. The contract was publicly announced on 7 October 1966 and provided $313,000 for fifteen months, 1 November 1966 to 31 January 1968; total funding later rose above $500,000.

The contract terms are worth reading against what followed. The report states that "the contract provided that the planning, direction and conclusions of the Colorado project were to be conducted wholly independently of the Air Force," that the Air Force was ordered to furnish its records and base support, and that "we were assured that the federal government would withhold no information on the subject." Where sightings involved classified missile launches or classified radar systems, "this fact is merely stated as to do more would involve violation of security on these military subjects." The committee then reports that these reservations "have affected a negligible fraction of the total material." This is an assurance accepted on the word of the contracting party, by a project that had no independent means of verifying either the completeness of what it received or the existence of holdings outside Blue Book.

The Low memorandum predates the contract by two months. Written 9 August 1966 to two university administrators, it reassured them that the study "would be conducted almost entirely by non-believers who, though they couldn't possibly prove a negative result, could and probably would add an impressive body of thick evidence that there is no reality to the observations," before the sentence about the trick. James McDonald learned of it in July 1967 and located a copy in the project's own open files; NICAP severed ties on 30 April 1968; Donald Keyhoe circulated copies; John G. Fuller published "Flying Saucer Fiasco" in Look on 14 May 1968, describing the project as a "$500,000 trick." Condon fired David Saunders and Norman Levine for alleged incompetence; administrative assistant Mary Louise Armstrong resigned; Low resigned in May 1968. Representative J. Edward Roush asked the General Accounting Office to investigate; GAO declined. Condon resigned from the AAAS after Science published on the controversy without his input.

What the committee produced is not a single argument but a document whose front matter contradicts its interior. Condon's six-page Conclusions and Recommendations opens: "Our general conclusion is that nothing has come from the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge. Careful consideration of the record as it is available to us leads us to conclude that further extensive study of UFOs probably cannot be justified in the expectation that science will be advanced thereby." He recommended against a new federal agency, and on secrecy wrote: "It has been contended that the subject has been shrouded in official secrecy. We conclude otherwise. We have no evidence of secrecy concerning UFO reports. What has been miscalled secrecy has been no more than an intelligent policy of delay in releasing data so that the public does not become confused by premature publication of incomplete studies of reports."

Set that against the adjacent paragraphs. On the defense question Condon wrote: "We felt that it was out of our province to attempt an independent evaluation of this conclusion. We adopted the attitude that, without attempting to assume the defense responsibility which is that of the Air Force, if we came across any evidence whatever that seemed to us to indicate a defense hazard we would call it to the attention of the Air Force at once. We did not find any such evidence. We know of no reason to question the finding of the Air Force." The committee thus deferred to the Air Force on the national-security question and then, three paragraphs later, certified that no secrecy existed. Hynek's later count was that the committee had been unable to explain more than a quarter of the cases it examined. In Case 2 of Section IV, Chapter 2, on the 1956 Lakenheath-Bentwaters radar-visual event, the report states: "although conventional or natural explanations certainly cannot be ruled out, the probability of such seems low in this case and the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved appears to be fairly high."

The operational effect was immediate and durable. The Air Force had asked the National Academy of Sciences, before the report was finished, to independently assess its scope, methodology and findings; a panel chaired by Yale astronomer Gerald M. Clemence studied it for six weeks and endorsed it, concluding that "no high priority in UFO investigations is warranted by data of the past two decades." On 17 December 1969 the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project Blue Book, citing the Colorado report, the NAS review, past studies and Air Force experience. The Air Force fact sheet distributed from Wright-Patterson in January 1985 records the closing tally — 12,618 sightings reported 1947 to 1969, of which 701 remain "Unidentified" — and appends a categorical denial: "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base." That sentence, on a public affairs fact sheet from the base that housed ATIC and let the Battelle contract, is a dated, attributable claim about the specific installation most often named in recovery accounts. It is evidence about the denier.
