dossier.denialPosture: Condon's Section I contains one of the two most consequential official denials in the record: "We have no evidence of secrecy concerning UFO reports." It was issued by a body that had explicitly declined to evaluate the defense question, that acknowledged its access to classified missile and radar material was limited by the contracting agency, and whose project coordinator had described the public framing as a trick two months before the contract was signed. The Air Force's January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet supplies the companion denial about physical custody.
connections: Robertson Panel — a sanitized version of the panel report was published as Appendix Y of the Condon Report; Thornton Page sat on the Robertson Panel and later criticized Condon's statistical logic in the American Journal of Physics (vol. 37 no. 10, October 1969).

J. Allen Hynek — proposed the review that led to the O'Brien Committee, was rejected as a host institution, and became the report's leading critic, writing that the committee could not explain more than a quarter of the cases examined.
James E. McDonald (University of Arizona) — surfaced the Low memo in July 1967 and published "Science in Default" on 27 December 1969; he is a named node for the board's researcher-fate thread.

Air Force Office of Scientific Research — the contracting activity; Dr. J. Thomas Ratchford and AFOSR executive director Dr. William Price are the named officials who recruited Colorado in July-August 1966.
Brian O'Brien and the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board — the mechanism by which the Air Force generated the recommendation it then used to retire its own program.
National Academy of Sciences panel under Gerald M. Clemence — the independent validator, retained by the Air Force before the report was complete.
Project Blue Book / Wright-Patterson AFB — terminated on the strength of this report; its records went to NARA as microfilm publication T-1206, 94 rolls.
Air Force Regulation 80-17, reproduced as Appendix B, is the base-level UFO reporting procedure the same review created and the Air Force rescinded on Blue Book's closure.
AARO — the first federal UFO office since Condon recommended against creating one; the fifty-three-year gap between the two is the concealment window this board examines.
openQuestions: The report states the Air Force assured the project that no information would be withheld. No document memorializing that assurance, and no accounting of what classified missile or radar material was in fact withheld, has been produced.
Was the Colorado project given access to anything outside the Blue Book file series — ATIC's Battelle-era holdings, foreign technology division files, or any compartmented program?

Condon stated in a January 1967 lecture that he thought the government should not study UFOs because the subject was nonsense, "but I'm not supposed to reach that conclusion for another year." Who, if anyone, in the Air Force knew of that statement at the time?
The GAO declined Rep. Roush's request to investigate the project. On what stated grounds, and does a written GAO declination exist?
Fifty-nine case studies were published with their locations altered "for legal reasons." The key mapping location-to-case has never been released.
Low resigned in May 1968; no further contemporaneous account of the August 1966 memo's audience or purpose has surfaced.
Why did the Air Force commission an NAS review of the report before the report was finished?

l0.label: The Wilson-Davis Notes (16 October 2002)

dossier.whatItIs: A 15-page document consisting of meeting notes attributed to Dr. Eric W. Davis, headed "Eric Davis Meeting with Adm. Wilson" and dated 10/16/02, purporting to record an approximately seventy-minute conversation with recently retired Vice Adm. Thomas R. Wilson - former Deputy Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency and Assistant Joint Chief of Staff J-2, and Director of DIA from 1999 until July 2002. The notes place the conversation in Wilson's parked car behind the EG&G Special Projects building at Grier and Paradise in Las Vegas. The document is said to have surfaced from the estate of Apollo 14 astronaut Edgar Mitchell following his death in February 2016 and circulated online from 2019. Its provenance is contested and Wilson has denied the meeting on the record. Critical handling note: the version in general circulation is an annotated PDF prepared by an anonymous third party, and the marginal identifications of Lockheed Martin as the unnamed contractor and of Noel Longuemare Jr. as the Senior Review Group chairman are the annotator's inferences, not statements attributed to Wilson anywhere in the notes.
dossier.whyImplicated: If authentic, this is the single most operationally specific description in the open record of how a legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering effort would be insulated from oversight - and it is specific in ways that are checkable. It describes a special projects record group inside the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Technology that sat outside the SAP divisions William Perry reorganised in 1994. It names the officials Wilson allegedly worked through: Perry, Under Secretary Paul Kaminski, Brig. Gen. Michael Kostelnik as director of special programs and SAPCO director and executive secretary to SAPOC, Maj. Gen. H. Marshal Ward, Judith Daly at OUSD(A&T), and Jacques Gansler on arrival in December 1997. It describes a contractor-side committee of program director, security director and corporate attorney - calling itself "the watch committee" - administering access criteria that overrode a serving three-star's statutory need-to-know, and a bigot list dated 1990 and updated 1993 covering 400 to 800 workers containing no politicians, no White House names and no congressional staffers. And it describes the enforcement mechanism: the SAPOC Senior Review Group sustaining the contractor and warning Wilson he would lose his promotion and one or two stars. If it is a fabrication, that is equally load-bearing, because the fabricator understood SAP governance vocabulary well enough that the document was later entered into a congressional hearing record.
dossier.narrative:
The document must be handled as three separable things: an artifact with a physical history, a set of assertions about 1997, and a contested attribution. Keeping them separate is what makes it usable.

As an artifact, its most consequential fact is institutional. The Internet Archive copy of the annotated memo cites, as its provenance, the congressional document HHRG-117-IG05-20220517-SD001 posted at congress.gov under the 17 May 2022 hearing of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Subcommittee on Counterterrorism, Counterintelligence and Counterproliferation - the first open congressional UAP hearing in over fifty years. Reporting indicates Rep. Mike Gallagher raised the document with the Pentagon witnesses and obtained unanimous consent to enter it into the record. Whatever its authenticity, it is now a document in a congressional hearing file, and its assertions are therefore assertions Congress has formally received and not adjudicated.

As a set of assertions, the notes describe a search rather than a revelation. Wilson, then Deputy Director of DIA and Assistant JCS J-2, is depicted as acting after an April 1997 Pentagon conference-room briefing given by Steven Greer, Cmdr. Willard Miller and Edgar Mitchell, at which Adm. Mike Crawford and Wilson's superior Lt. Gen. Patrick Hughes were present. Wilson and Miller then spoke privately for two hours about, in the memo's phrasing, UFOs, MJ-12, Roswell, crashed UFOs and alien bodies. Wilson is described as already knowing of intelligence on US military and foreign government close encounters. Over roughly forty-five days he made calls, was pointed by Maj. Gen. Ward and by Perry toward the records groups in OUSD(A&T), located what he describes as a special projects record group that did not belong to the usual SAP divisions as organised by Perry in 1994, and read the index abstracts. He is described as being told by Kostelnik that program security costs ran two to three times the program budget and at times six to seven times core budget, that Perry had wanted an investigation of that ratio and was told to drop it, and that Judith Daly explained the discrepancy as a records-keeping artifact of cumulative versus annual reporting.

What follows is the part that is genuinely novel in the UFO literature, because it is not about a craft. It is about jurisdiction. Wilson is described as making three calls to the program manager, one a conference call with a security director and a corporate attorney, and then flying out ten days later to meet the same three in a secure vault. They call themselves "the watch committee" or gatekeepers, and explain that they formed after an earlier audit investigation nearly exposed them, following which a formal agreement was struck with SAPOC establishing special access criteria administered by the contractor committee rather than by the government, such that no USG personnel gain access unless the contractor's criteria are met "irregardless of the tickets and position USG personnel possessed." Wilson's regulatory and statutory authority as Deputy Director DIA is declared not relevant to their program. He is shown a bigot list several pages long, dated 1990 and updated 1993, mostly program employees, civilians, with a handful of recognisable Pentagon names from OUSD(A&T), one from another department, and one at the NSC who was a Pentagon SES employee. No politicians. No White House. No Congress.

Only then does the substance appear, and it is brief: the program manager states they are not a weapons, intelligence, special operations or logistics program; that they are a reverse engineering program; that something was recovered years ago; that they have an intact craft they believe could fly; that it did not come from overseas and could not have; that they did not know where it was from; that it was "technology that was not of this Earth - not made by man - not by human hands"; that progress had been agonisingly slow with painful lack of outside collaboration; and that the bigot-list workforce ran about 400 to 800 people varying with funding. On Roswell, Holloman, MJ-12 and Zamora and Bentwaters, they declined to discuss. Wilson threatened to escalate to SAPOC, did so, and the Senior Review Group sustained the contractor twice, told him to drop it, and - per the memo - the chairman warned he would not see the DIA director promotion, would get early retirement, and would lose one or two stars. In January 1998 Wilson is described as raising his June 1997 meetings with the new Under Secretary Jacques Gansler, who had somehow been briefed, and who said: "UFOs are real, so-called 'alien abductions' not real."

As a contested attribution, the record is unambiguous on one side and silent on the other. Wilson has denied it directly, telling a reporter it is all fiction, that he would not know Eric Davis if he walked in, and that he did not sit in a car with him in Las Vegas for an hour; he says he told both a Senate staffer and AARO that Davis is making it up. Davis has declined to comment publicly on the document since it appeared. Individuals identified in the memo as arranging the meeting are reported to have denied knowing Wilson. And AARO's own Historical Record Report Volume 1, the government's most extensive published treatment of exactly these allegations, does not contain the name Wilson anywhere in its 1,500-plus lines of text - it disposes of the entire category by asserting that claims involving specific people, locations, tests and documents are inaccurate and largely the product of circular reporting, without engaging this document at all. A critical handling note: the widely circulated PDF is an annotated version, and the marginal identification of Lockheed Martin as the unnamed contractor is the anonymous annotator's inference, not anything attributed to Wilson in the notes.

claims.text: The Internet Archive copy of the annotated memo identifies its provenance as "Part of the US Congressional Record" at https://www.congress.gov/117/meeting/house/114761/documents/HHRG-117-IG05-20220517-SD001.pdf, the document file for the 17 May 2022 House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence subcommittee UAP hearing. Reporting indicates Rep. Mike Gallagher raised the document at that hearing and obtained unanimous consent to enter it into the record as SD001.

The document is dated 10/16/02, headed "Eric Davis Meeting with Adm. Wilson," and records the meeting as taking place at the EG&G Special Projects building at Grier and Paradise, with the conversation held in Wilson's car behind the EG&G building until 11:20 A.M.
claims.source: Wilson-Davis memo, 16 October 2002, p.1; full text at https://archive.org/stream/annotated_wilson_memo/annotated_wilson_memo_djvu.txt

claims.text: The memo records the contractor program manager stating the program was "a reverse engineering program," that "They had a craft - an intact craft they believed could fly," and that "it was technology that was not of this Earth - not made by man - not by human hands."

The memo names Maj. Gen. H. Marshal Ward and Secretary William Perry as the sources of the suggestion to search records-group files in OUSD(A&T), and identifies Paul Kaminski as Under Secretary of Defense (Acquisition and Technology) and Brig. Gen. Michael Kostelnik as director of special programs in OUSD(A&T), director of the Special Access Programs Coordination Office (SAPCO), executive secretary to the Special Access Programs Oversight Committee (SAPOC), and a member of the Senior Review Group. The memo states that what Wilson found there was "a special projects record group not belonging to usual SAP - a special subset of the unacknowledged/carve-outs/waived programs - not belonging to usual SAP divisions as organized in '94 by Perry himself - set apart from rest but buried/covered by conventional SAPs."

The memo records that program security spending ran "like 2-3 times the program budget, but there were times when it went as high as 6-7 times core budget," that Perry wanted an investigation of the ratio and "was told to drop it," and names Judith Daly, Assistant Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Advanced Development, OUSD(A&T), as the official who explained the figures as cumulative rather than annual security budget reporting.

The memo describes three contractor officials - a program director, a security director identified as NSA-retired and a counterintelligence expert, and a corporate attorney - who "Called themselves 'the watch committee,' or gate keepers," and who told Wilson that access criteria were "to be administered by contractor committee... irregardless of the tickets and position USG personnel possessed," and that "Regulatory and statutory authority as Deputy Director DIA not relevant or pertinent to nature of their program."

The memo records a bigot list "several pages long - dated 1990, updated 1993," comprising mostly civilian program employees, containing no politicians, no White House names, no President, no Congressional people and no Congressional staffers, but including "a handful of names" of Pentagon individuals Wilson recognised - some from OUSD(A&T), one from another department and one at the National Security Council who was a Pentagon SES employee - and a workforce of "about 400-800 (bigot list count) workers varying in number with funding or personnel changes."

The memo records Wilson identifying the holder only as "An aerospace technology contractor - one of the top ones in US," "the best one of them," with intelligence "In their corporate portfolio," and refusing to name it, the program compartment or the code name, each time on the grounds that it was a "core secret."

The memo records that after Wilson complained to the SAPOC Senior Review Group, its members sustained the contractor's access denial twice, told him "to immediately drop the matter and let it go," and that the Senior Review Group chairman warned that if he did not comply he "would not see Director DIA promotion, get early retirement, lose 1 or 2 stars along the way."

The memo records Wilson quoting incoming Under Secretary of Defense (Acquisition and Technology) Jacques Gansler, in a January 1998 conversation about the June 1997 meetings, as saying "UFOs are real, so-called 'alien abductions' not real," and then telling Wilson to drop the matter.

The memo package includes an attached letter from Cmdr. Willard 'Will' Miller dated 25 April 2002, addressed to "Dr. Eric W. Davis, CEO, Warp Drive Metrics, 4849 San Rafael Ave., Las Vegas, NV 89120," offering to supply "A list of civilian government contractors who, by virtue of their past and current highly classified work... most likely have current involvement in and knowledge of USG work in alien-derived technologies, crashes, landing, and associated events" at "$180 per straight-time hour."
claims.source: Miller to Davis, 25 April 2002, reproduced in the Wilson-Davis memo package, pp.3-5; https://archive.org/stream/annotated_wilson_memo/annotated_wilson_memo_djvu.txt

claims.text: Adm. Thomas Wilson has denied the meeting on the record, telling a reporter "It's all fiction" and "I wouldn't know Eric Davis if he walked in right now... I don't remember him, and I definitely did not sit with him in a car for an hour in Las Vegas," and states he told both a Senate staffer and AARO that Davis is making it all up. Eric Davis has declined to comment publicly on the document.

AARO's Historical Record Report Volume 1 (8 March 2024) does not contain the name 'Wilson' anywhere in its text and does not address this document by name, while stating that "AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology" and that the claim is "in large part, the result of circular reporting from a group of individuals."

Individuals identified in reporting as having set up the alleged meeting have stated they did not know Adm. Wilson and would not have facilitated a meeting between him and Davis; identifying and interviewing the 'Rich' and 'Doug' named in the memo as AFIO members who arranged the Nevada trip is the most direct available authentication test.

dossier.denialPosture: Wilson denies both the meeting and its substance in unqualified terms and says he has repeated the denial to a Senate staffer and to AARO. The memo itself anticipates exactly this, recording Wilson saying "If you blow my trust I'll deny meeting you, deny everything said, won't meet with any more people (without clearances) to talk about this topic" - which makes the denial non-diagnostic in either direction. Davis has neither authenticated nor repudiated the document publicly. AARO's most detailed published treatment of the reverse-engineering allegations does not mention Wilson or the memo at all, disposing of the category by reference to circular reporting rather than by addressing the artifact.
connections: Vice Adm. Thomas R. Wilson: Deputy Director DIA and Assistant Joint Chief of Staff J-2 in 1997, Director of DIA 1999 to July 2002, succeeded by Vice Adm. Lowell E. Jacoby; his superior in 1997 was Lt. Gen. Patrick M. Hughes, then Director DIA

Dr. Eric W. Davis: CEO of Warp Drive Metrics in 2002 per the attached Miller letter, later of EarthTech International with Harold Puthoff, and an author of AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Documents

Leslie Kean and the Boston Globe articles are named in the memo as the leak path that made Wilson furious with Miller
openQuestions: The chain of custody from the alleged 2002 note-taking to the Edgar Mitchell estate to the 2019 online release has never been documented
Whether an unannotated original bearing Davis's handwriting exists and has been examined by anyone independent
Whether the congressional submission was accompanied by any authentication, and who submitted it to the committee
Whether Kostelnik, Ward, Daly, Gansler or Kaminski have ever been asked about the memo's assertions on the record or under oath

The identity of the audit investigation the 'watch committee' says nearly exposed them, and the terms of the formal agreement with SAPOC that followed

l0.label: UAP Science Advisory Council

dossier.whatItIs: The UAP Science Advisory Council is an outside scientific advisory body assembled in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the FBI and other agencies, and chaired by Harvard theoretical physicist Avi Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board that met for the first time in mid-June 2026. All data shared with the council is unclassified.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject, which makes the terms on which it was convened the most informative thing about it. Its chair has stated in writing that 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' A body with no clearances and no access to classified holdings cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a special access programme operating under a DCSA carve-out, cannot compel testimony, and cannot verify a negative. Its function, on the record as constituted, is to apply scientific method to the portion of the record that nobody disputes and that the executive branch has already chosen to release. Its membership was drawn almost entirely from the private technical and advocacy layer - the Sol Foundation and the Galileo Project - rather than from the federal laboratories, FFRDCs or prime contractors where the custody allegations point, and the published membership lists changed three times in seventeen days.
dossier.narrative:
The council is best understood as a boundary object: an institution created at the seam between a declassification programme and a scientific community, whose terms of reference tell you exactly where the executive branch has decided that seam sits.

The origin story is not disputed by anyone involved. The Skeptics Society announcement of 15 June 2026 says the council was 'formed at the request of the White House and in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and other agencies.' Avi Loeb's own account, published on Medium and dated by the platform to 13 June 2026, says: 'Over the past week, I was tasked by the above organizations to create a research team of young scientists who will serve on this council,' naming the White House, AARO, ODNI, the FBI and all Intelligence Community members. The Sol Foundation's account says ODNI, with the support of the FBI, announced it. DefenseScoop obtained confirmation from an ODNI official that ODNI, alongside the FBI and DoD, established the UAP Governance Board 'to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies,' and that the board 'met for the first time yesterday' as of Wednesday 17 June 2026, without identifying the participants.

The membership is where the record becomes genuinely strange, and the board should record the instability rather than smoothing it into a single roster. Loeb's first post named a core research team of five: Richard Cloete, Regina Sarmiento, Matthew Szydagis, Devesh Nandal and Omer Eldadi. The Skeptics Society, two days later, published an alphabetised list of eleven, adding Tim Gallaudet, Garry Nolan, Michael Shermer, Peter Skafish and Jennice Vilhauer, and identifying Loeb as chair. The Sol Foundation described a fourteen-member council and additionally named Jacob Haqq-Misra and Ross Howard. Loeb's list supplied to DefenseScoop on 17 June named twelve and introduced Carol Cleland and Ben Lamm while dropping Sarmiento. His second Medium post, dated by the platform to 29 June, listed fifteen and added Liberty Vittert Capito, Robin Hanson and Kevin Knuth while restoring none of the dropped names. Four published lists in seventeen days, none of them identical, none of them issued by the government that convened the body. There is no charter, no Federal Advisory Committee Act notice, and no agency-published membership roster in the record reviewed here.

The operative constraint is stated by the chair himself, twice, in plain language: 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The Sol Foundation repeats it. DefenseScoop reports that Loeb 'confirmed that all of the data shared with the newly installed team will be unclassified.' Loeb also told DefenseScoop that the meeting cadence has not been decided, and closed with a formulation that is worth quoting exactly because it is candid about the position: 'We will make the best lemonade out of the lemons we are given.'

Set that against what the council would need in order to test the central allegation on this board. The custody claims concern material held at contractor facilities under special access protection. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), the Director of DCSA can be relieved of industrial security oversight of exactly such a facility by a Deputy Secretary of Defense-approved carve-out. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee may hand SAP material to a member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. A council with no clearances is on the outside of both of those doors. It cannot look at a carve-out programme, cannot subpoena a contractor, cannot inspect material, and cannot verify that the archival material it is given is complete. Its chair says the council's purpose is to advise on how to resolve the nature of UAP and, in support of the Governance Board, to 'assist in the timely coordination of declassification of UAP-related information, in accordance with Executive Order 13526.' That is a real function. It is also, structurally, an advisory role over the release of material that the classification authorities have already decided to release.

The second structural observation is about where the people came from. Loeb chairs the Galileo Project at Harvard; Cloete and Sarmiento are described in the Skeptics Society announcement as Galileo Project researchers. Nolan and Skafish co-founded the Sol Foundation; Gallaudet is a Sol senior adviser; Haqq-Misra sits on Sol's advisory board; Ross Howard leads Sol's production and was named to lead the council's communications. Nobody named to the council in any published list is identified as coming from a federal weapons laboratory, an FFRDC, a University Affiliated Research Center, or a prime contractor's advanced development organisation. The council is staffed from the community that has been asking the questions, not from the institutions that would hold the answers.

None of that is a criticism of the individuals, several of whom have argued publicly for exactly the kind of instrumentation and data quality that would move this subject forward. It is a statement about the shape of the instrument. The government convened an outside body, gave it distinguished members and a reporting line to an interagency board, and drew the boundary of its access at the classification line - the same line on the far side of which every substantive allegation this board catalogues is alleged to sit.

claims.text: The UAP Science Advisory Council was, per the Skeptics Society announcement of 15 June 2026, 'formed at the request of the White House and in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and other agencies.'

Avi Loeb wrote that 'Over the past week, I was tasked by the above organizations to create a research team of young scientists who will serve on this council,' identifying the White House, AARO, ODNI, the FBI and all Intelligence Community members.
Loeb states in writing that 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.'

The council reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board whose mission, per Loeb, is 'to serve as an interagency body that can use each member's capabilities and unique authorities to cohesively address national security threats posed by UAP' and which 'will assist in the timely coordination of declassification of UAP-related information, in accordance with Executive Order 13526.'

An ODNI official told DefenseScoop that ODNI, alongside the FBI and DoD, established the UAP Governance Board 'to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies,' and that the board met for the first time on 16 June 2026, without identifying the participants.
Loeb's first published account named a core team of five: Richard Cloete, Regina Sarmiento, Matthew Szydagis, Devesh Nandal and Omer Eldadi.
The Skeptics Society published an alphabetised list of eleven appointees on 15 June 2026: Cloete, Gallaudet, Nandal, Nolan, Eldadi, Loeb (chair), Sarmiento, Shermer, Skafish, Szydagis and Vilhauer.

The list Loeb supplied to DefenseScoop on 17 June 2026 named twelve people, introducing Carol Cleland (anomaly identification), Ben Lamm (oceanography and biology) and Ross Howard (communication), and omitting Regina Sarmiento.

Loeb's second Medium post listed fifteen members, adding Liberty Vittert Capito (data analysis and statistics), Robin Hanson (statistics and economics) and Kevin Knuth (physics and instrumentation) to the DefenseScoop list.
Four differing membership lists for the council were published between 13 and 29 June 2026, none of them identical to another and none of them issued by any of the agencies that convened the body.
Loeb told DefenseScoop that 'The frequency of the council's meeting cadence has not been decided' and that 'We will make the best lemonade out of the lemons we are given.'
The Sol Foundation independently states that the council has fourteen members, reports to the UAP Governance Board, and that all data shared with it will be unclassified.

No person named to the council in any of the four published lists is identified as coming from a federal weapons laboratory, an FFRDC, a University Affiliated Research Center, or a prime contractor's advanced development organisation; the membership is drawn from the Galileo Project, the Sol Foundation, academia and science communication.

No charter, Federal Advisory Committee Act notice, agency-published membership roster, or terms of reference for the UAP Science Advisory Council or the UAP Governance Board has been located in the public record.

dossier.denialPosture: The council itself has issued no denial. Its chair has repeatedly and publicly stated its principal limitation rather than concealing it: all data shared with the council is unclassified. AARO, one of the convening agencies, maintains in its published reporting that no US government investigation has found a case of UAP representing off-world technology, and that all authentic programmes referenced by whistleblowers were properly notified and reported to the congressional defence and intelligence committees.
openQuestions: Whether the council has a charter, terms of reference, or FACA status, and whether its membership has ever been published by a government agency rather than by members and third parties.
The definitive membership. Four published lists in seventeen days disagree; the government has published none.
Whether any council member holds a security clearance in another capacity, and whether that creates an asymmetry inside a body constituted to work on unclassified material only.
The identity of the participants in the UAP Governance Board, which ODNI declined to share, and the board's own authorities over declassification decisions.

Whether the council has any mechanism to determine that the archival material it receives is complete, or is dependent on the classification authorities whose conduct is the subject of the underlying allegations.

l0.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (UAPTF)

dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (UAPTF) was a Department of Defense body approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense David L. Norquist on 4 August 2020 and announced publicly on 14 August 2020, led by the Department of the Navy under the cognizance of the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. Its stated mission was to detect, analyze and catalog UAP that could potentially pose a threat to U.S. national security. It produced the dataset behind the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment and was superseded in November 2021 by AOIMSG and in 2022 by AARO.
dossier.whyImplicated: The UAPTF is where the modern disclosure fight acquired its documents and its witnesses. David Grusch served as the National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAPTF, and it was from inside that role that he says he was briefed on, and then denied access to, a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program. That is the specific institutional pathway by which a legacy program's existence leaked into a body that Congress could subpoena. The task force also demonstrates the concealment mechanism in miniature: a Navy-led, OUSD(I&S)-supervised body with an unclassified public face and a classified annex, stood up only after decades of the same phenomena being handled through channels Congress was not shown. Within fifteen months of its public announcement it was dissolved and its functions moved twice, each time into a differently named organization with different reporting lines. Reorganization is a documented concealment technique on this board, and the UAPTF-to-AOIMSG-to-AARO chain is the cleanest recent example of it.
dossier.narrative:
The establishment is on the record and unambiguous. The Navy's own press release of 14 August 2020 states: "On Aug. 4, 2020, Deputy Secretary of Defense David L. Norquist approved the establishment of an Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Task Force (UAPTF). The Department of the Navy, under the cognizance of the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, will lead the UAPTF." The mission statement is "to detect, analyze and catalog UAPs that could potentially pose a threat to U.S. national security." Note what is absent: any reference to materials, recoveries, or prior programs. The public charter is a sensor-and-safety charter.

What the UAPTF actually produced was the dataset in the ODNI preliminary assessment delivered 25 June 2021, prepared in response to a reporting provision attached to the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. That nine-page unclassified assessment, with a classified annex, covers 144 reports from U.S. government sources between November 2004 and March 2021, states that most reports came from Navy and other military aviators, and identifies a small number of cases where UAP "appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, maneuver abruptly, or move at considerable speed, without discernable means of propulsion." The assessment explicitly declines to attribute the phenomena and cites limited, inconsistent reporting as the principal analytic constraint. It is the government's own written acknowledgment that a body of unexplained aerospace observations exists inside its own sensor record.

The personnel question is where the task force becomes load-bearing for the program argument. David Grusch, an Air Force veteran and intelligence officer, served as the NRO representative to the UAPTF from 2019 to 2021 and then as his agency's co-lead for UAP and trans-medium object analysis at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency from 2021 to 2023. In 2022 he filed a complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General that was found credible and urgent for reporting to the congressional intelligence committees. On 26 July 2023, under oath before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, Grusch testified that in the course of his official duties he was informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program to which he was denied access, and that recoveries included non-human biologics. Whatever one concludes about the substance, the provenance is institutional: the claim entered the public record through a person whose job was to represent a national intelligence agency to a DoD task force.

The dissolution is as instructive as the founding. On 23 November 2021 Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, directed the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security to establish the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group as the successor to the Navy's UAPTF, with oversight from an Airborne Object Identification and Management Executive Council drawn from DoD and the intelligence community. Ronald Moultrie was the USD(I&S) of record. AOIMSG itself lasted months before being reconstituted in July 2022 as the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. Three names, three charters, three sets of reporting relationships, in under two years, for the same subject matter. Each transition reset what Congress had been briefed on and who owed the briefing.

The naming precision matters here in the same way it matters for AATIP. The UAPTF was a Navy-led DoD task force with an OUSD(I&S) reporting chain. It was not a special access program, it did not have acquisition authority, and nothing in its public charter gives it custody of anything. That is precisely Grusch's point: he says the compartmented activity he learned about was adjacent to, and walled off from, the body Congress had been told was handling the subject. The UAPTF is therefore best read on this board not as the program but as the sensor that detected the program from inside the building.

Who matters by name: Norquist (approving authority), Hicks (dissolving authority), Moultrie (USD(I&S)), Grusch (NRO representative), and the ODNI and Navy officials who signed out the June 2021 assessment. What the record shows is a legitimate, publicly chartered analytic body producing a public product that concedes unexplained observations. What the record does not show is any UAPTF authority over, or access to, materials — and the absence of that authority in a body specifically created to be the government's answer on UAP is the anomaly worth pulling on.

claims.text: Deputy Secretary of Defense David L. Norquist approved establishment of the UAP Task Force on 4 August 2020; the Department of the Navy, under the cognizance of the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, was designated to lead it.
The establishment was announced publicly on 14 August 2020.
The UAPTF mission of record is 'to detect, analyze and catalog UAPs that could potentially pose a threat to U.S. national security.'
The Office of the Director of National Intelligence published 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena' on 25 June 2021, drawing on UAPTF work.
The 25 June 2021 ODNI assessment covers 144 reports originating from U.S. government sources, primarily U.S. military aviators, for incidents occurring between November 2004 and March 2021.
The 25 June 2021 ODNI assessment was accompanied by a classified annex; the unclassified body attributes only one of the 144 reports with high confidence.

On 23 November 2021 Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks directed the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security to establish the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group (AOIMSG) as successor to the Navy's UAP Task Force, with an Airborne Object Identification and Management Executive Council (AOIMEXEC) providing oversight.
claims.source: OSD(PA) briefing card, 'AOIMSG Establishment, November 23, 2021', released under DoD FOIA 22-F-0381: https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/FOID/Reading%20Room/UFOsandUAPs/22-F-0381_PA_AOIMSG_Briefing_Cards_05-22-23.pdf

claims.text: AOIMSG was placed under the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, then held by Ronald Moultrie.
AOIMSG was superseded in July 2022 by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), producing three differently named organizations covering the same subject matter within a 24-month period.

David Grusch served as the National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAP Task Force from 2019 to 2021, and from 2021 to 2023 as his agency's co-lead for UAP and trans-medium object analysis at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.
In 2022 Grusch filed a whistleblower complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General that was found credible and urgent for transmission to the congressional intelligence committees.

On 26 July 2023 Grusch testified under oath before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, describing himself as a former NRO representative to the UAP Task Force and stating he had been informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program to which he was denied access.
claims.source: House hearing 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency,' 26 July 2023: https://www.congress.gov/event/118th-congress/house-event/116282

claims.text: AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 states that AARO 'has no evidence for the USG reverse-engineering narrative provided by interviewees' and assesses that named alleged reverse-engineering programs either do not exist, are misidentified authentic sensitive programs, or resolve to 'an unwarranted and disestablished program.'
The UAPTF's public charter as published contains no reference to materials custody, acquisition authority, or reverse engineering; its stated functions are detection, analysis and cataloguing.

dossier.denialPosture: DoD has never denied the UAPTF existed; it published its own establishment. The denial operates one level down, at AARO, which states in its 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 that it has found no evidence of any U.S. reverse-engineering program and that interviewees, including those with UAPTF-adjacent access, 'likely' misinterpreted sensitive but conventional programs because 'none of the interviewees had firsthand knowledge.' The denial is an assertion about the mental states of named witnesses rather than a document production.
connections: David Norquist and Kathleen Hicks: consecutive Deputy Secretaries who created and dissolved the same body. The Hicks name also appears on the DoD side of the 2023-2024 KONA BLUE declassification correspondence with DHS.
David Grusch's UAPTF billet is the documented conduit between the compartmented world and the House Oversight Committee. He is the single node linking NRO, NGA, UAPTF, the ICIG, and the 2023 hearing.
Ronald Moultrie (USD(I&S)) supervised both the UAPTF's parent office and AOIMSG, and testified before Congress on UAP in 2022.
Luis Elizondo's claimed OUSD(I) AATIP activity and the UAPTF share the same OUSD(I&S) reporting chain a decade apart.

The ODNI preliminary assessment's classified annex is the unreleased counterpart to a public document that Congress has repeatedly cited; it is the most concretely identified withheld UAP record in the modern era.

AARO, the third-generation successor, is the entity that later issued the KONA BLUE narrative and the Historical Record Report, meaning the successor to the task force is also the author of the government's denial.
The FY2024 NDAA UAP Records Collection at NARA is the statutory downstream of records the UAPTF generated.
openQuestions: The 4 August 2020 Norquist approval memorandum itself has not been released in full. What does the charter say beyond the press release summary?
Who led the UAPTF day to day, and what was the size and composition of its staff? DoD has never published a roster.
What is in the classified annex to the 25 June 2021 ODNI assessment, and has it been provided to the House Oversight Committee?
Was there an ONI-run UAP task force predating the 4 August 2020 formalization, and if so under what authority did it operate?
Grusch says he was briefed on a program while serving as NRO representative to the UAPTF. Who briefed him, and does the UAPTF hold a record of that briefing?
What happened to UAPTF holdings during the two reorganizations, and were any records destroyed or reclassified in transit?

l0.label: PURSUE - Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters

dossier.whatItIs: PURSUE - the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters - is the Department of War's UAP file-release programme, published at war.gov/UFO and launched with a first tranche on 8 May 2026. It stands on a presidential direction issued by Donald Trump on Truth Social on 19 February 2026 rather than on a statute or a published executive order, and it is run by the Department of War with support from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence across an interagency group that includes the White House, the Department of Energy, AARO, NASA and the FBI.
dossier.whyImplicated: PURSUE is the first time the executive branch has conceded, in its own words on its own website, that UAP records were 'hidden behind classifications' and that there are 'tens of millions of records' to review. That concession is the argument. It was made not by AARO, the office Congress created to resolve UAP, but over AARO's head by the Secretary of War at the direction of the President, through a portal that is not aaro.mil and a process that is not FOIA, not mandatory declassification review, and not the National Archives collection Congress legislated in 2023. AARO's role was reduced to preparing other agencies' files for posting on someone else's website. And the programme's declared editorial posture - a War Department official told DefenseScoop 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file' - means the government has published imagery while withholding the analysis it certainly holds, which is the precise shape of a controlled release rather than a disclosure.
dossier.narrative:
On 19 February 2026 the President posted on Truth Social. The Department of War now reproduces the text on its own UAP portal as the programme's founding instrument: 'Based on the tremendous interest shown, I will be directing the Secretary of War, and other relevant Departments and Agencies, to begin the process of identifying and releasing Government files related to alien and extraterrestrial life, unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP), and unidentified flying objects (UFOs), and any and all other information connected to these highly complex, but extremely interesting and important, matters. GOD BLESS AMERICA!' There is no executive order number on the page. There is no statutory citation. The authority for the largest UAP declassification effort in American history, as presented by the Department itself, is a social media post.

The portal's Directive section states what the Department says it is doing: 'In response to President Donald J. Trump's directive for transparency on U.S. government information regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), the Department of War (DOW), with support from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), is overseeing government wide efforts to expeditiously find, review, identify, declassify and publicly release unresolved UAP-related records and historical documents in the federal government's possession. This is an unprecedented, historic undertaking that requires coordination between dozens of agencies and the review of tens of millions of records, many existing only on paper, spanning many decades.' It commits to 'releasing new materials on a rolling basis as they are discovered and declassified, with tranches posted every few weeks.'

The scope limitation is stated in the next paragraph and is doing more work than it appears to: 'The materials archived here are unresolved cases, meaning the government is unable to make a definitive determination on the nature of the observed phenomena.' PURSUE publishes only what the government has failed to explain. It does not publish the resolved cases, the analytic products, or the compartmented holdings. 'DOW will continue to conduct separate reporting on resolved UAP cases, as mandated by statute.' The statutory channel and the presidential channel are explicitly separated, and the presidential channel gets the unexplained material.

The interagency composition, from the 8 May press release, is: 'The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the Department of Energy (DOE), the DOW's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and additional components of U.S. intelligence agencies.' The inclusion of the Department of Energy is the item on that list that should not be passed over: DOE is the custodian of the Restricted Data and transclassified foreign nuclear information regime that the Senate's own 2023 findings named as a mechanism by which UAP records escape mandatory declassification review.

The posture of the principals is uniform and quotable. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth: 'These files, hidden behind classifications, have long fueled justified speculation - and it's time the American people see it for themselves.' Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard described ODNI as 'actively coordinating the Intelligence Community's declassification efforts with the Department of War'. FBI Director Kash Patel: 'For the first time in history, the American people have unfettered access to declassified government files on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomenon.' NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman framed it as a whole-of-government effort. The 8 May release also contains a sentence that concedes the analytic gap up front: 'While all of the files have been reviewed for security purposes, many of the materials have not yet been analyzed for resolution of any anomalies.'

AARO's position in this architecture is the diagnostic fact. A War Department official told DefenseScoop: 'AARO is responsible for coordinating the declassification of identified DOW files. AARO also prepares DOW files and files provided by other agencies for posting on war.gov/ufo. AARO will continue to conduct its statutory mission of detecting, identifying, analyzing, and resolving UAP. Any encounters described in these releases that are resolved in the future will be posted on aaro.mil.' The statutory UAP office is a preparation function for a portal it does not own. DefenseScoop states the point flatly: batches are dropping on war.gov/ufo, 'not the existing aaro.mil website.' The war.gov portal's own 'Learn More' section reverses the flow, sending readers who want 'other historical UAP records' to aaro.mil.

And then the posture that defines the programme. Asked about the release, the War Department official said: 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file, so that the American people can make up their own minds regarding the files.' That sentence is presented as humility. Christopher Mellon, former deputy assistant secretary of defense for intelligence, identified what it actually is: 'For years the public was told there was little to see. The scale of what exists is itself a revelation. That said, data alone is not disclosure. Releasing raw files without context may confuse more than clarify.' Mellon's sharper formulation to DefenseScoop: 'The more substantive concern is not that the government is trying to overwhelm the public with low-quality data - it's that it is releasing evidence without releasing analysis.'

The technical complaint is the same complaint from every direction. Alejandro Rojas of Enigma Labs: 'Case summaries without coordinates, sensor parameters, or altitude data make independent analysis very difficult.' Retired Rear Adm. Tim Gallaudet: 'the ambiguity of the video content in particular is concerning as no metadata was included. Therefore, it is impossible to conclude that any of the objects were truly anomalous.' Ryan Graves: 'The real value is in records that include clear provenance, sensor context, metadata, chain of custody, date and location, and enough operational context to allow serious independent analysis.'

That is the shape of PURSUE. The Department of War admitted the archive exists, published the parts of it nobody can interpret, kept the analysis, kept the resolved cases, kept the compartments, and instructed the public to make up its own mind.

claims.text: The Department of War publishes the programme under the title 'Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE)' at war.gov/UFO.

The portal reproduces the presidential direction, dated 19 February 2026 and attributed to Truth Social: 'Based on the tremendous interest shown, I will be directing the Secretary of War, and other relevant Departments and Agencies, to begin the process of identifying and releasing Government files related to alien and extraterrestrial life, unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP), and unidentified flying objects (UFOs), and any and all other information connected to these highly complex, but extremely interesting and important, matters. GOD BLESS AMERICA!'

The portal's Directive states that the Department of War, 'with support from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), is overseeing government wide efforts to expeditiously find, review, identify, declassify and publicly release unresolved UAP-related records', an undertaking 'that requires coordination between dozens of agencies and the review of tens of millions of records, many existing only on paper, spanning many decades', with 'tranches posted every few weeks.'

The portal limits the collection's scope: 'The materials archived here are unresolved cases, meaning the government is unable to make a definitive determination on the nature of the observed phenomena', and states 'DOW will continue to conduct separate reporting on resolved UAP cases, as mandated by statute.'

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's published statement reads: 'The Department of War is in lockstep with President Trump to bring unprecedented transparency regarding our government's understanding of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena. These files, hidden behind classifications, have long fueled justified speculation - and it's time the American people see it for themselves.'

The 8 May 2026 Department of War release names the interagency participants as 'The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the Department of Energy (DOE), the DOW's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and additional components of U.S. intelligence agencies.'
The same release concedes: 'While all of the files have been reviewed for security purposes, many of the materials have not yet been analyzed for resolution of any anomalies.'

Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard's statement describes ODNI as 'actively coordinating the Intelligence Community's declassification efforts with the Department of War to ensure a careful, comprehensive, and unprecedented review of our holdings', and calls the 8 May release 'the first in what will be an ongoing joint declassification and release effort.'

A War Department official told DefenseScoop: 'AARO is responsible for coordinating the declassification of identified DOW files. AARO also prepares DOW files and files provided by other agencies for posting on war.gov/ufo. AARO will continue to conduct its statutory mission of detecting, identifying, analyzing, and resolving UAP. Any encounters described in these releases that are resolved in the future will be posted on aaro.mil.'

DefenseScoop reported on 14 May 2026 that PURSUE tranches are 'dropping on the new, centralized war.gov/ufo portal - not the existing aaro.mil website', and identified the acronym expansion as the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters.

A War Department official stated the programme's editorial posture: 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file, so that the American people can make up their own minds regarding the files.'

Christopher Mellon, former deputy assistant secretary of defense for intelligence, said of the first tranche: 'For years the public was told there was little to see. The scale of what exists is itself a revelation. That said, data alone is not disclosure. Releasing raw files without context may confuse more than clarify.' He added that 'it is releasing evidence without releasing analysis.'
The war.gov/UFO portal's 'Learn More' section directs readers seeking 'other historical UAP records' to aaro.mil, the statutory office's site, which is not the host of the PURSUE material.

PURSUE is not a statutory declassification process, not a FOIA channel and not the National Archives UAP Records Collection created by Public Law 118-31; it is a departmental publication programme run on the Secretary's web estate under a presidential direction announced on social media.
claims.source: Inference from https://www.war.gov/UFO/ (no statutory or executive order citation appears on the portal) set against Public Law 118-31 secs. 1841-1843 at https://www.congress.gov/118/plaws/publ31/PLAW-118publ31.pdf

dossier.denialPosture: The Department of War's declared posture is non-assessment: a War Department official told DefenseScoop that 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file.' The portal simultaneously asserts that the released material consists of unresolved cases the government 'is unable to make a definitive determination' on. Neither the Department nor ODNI has addressed whether any legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering programme records fall within the PURSUE search, and AARO's standing position that it has found no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial technology has not been withdrawn.
openQuestions: No executive order, memorandum or written tasking implementing the 19 February 2026 direction has been published; the legal instrument governing PURSUE is not on the public record.
What search terms, record series and agency components were tasked, and whether special access program holdings were within scope at all.
Which office adjudicates redactions and under which exemption authority, given that no FOIA case numbers or exemption citations appear on the released material.
Whether the Department of Energy's participation extends to Restricted Data or transclassified foreign nuclear information holdings, the exemption route the Senate identified in 2023.
Whether any records were withheld in full, and whether a withholding log exists.
Whether AARO's preparation role gives it the ability to exclude material originated by other DoW components before posting.

l0.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)

dossier.whatItIs: The Department of Defense, renamed the Department of War by executive action in 2025, is the cabinet department that has run every official US government UAP investigation from Project SIGN in December 1947 to AARO today. It holds the special access programme architecture, the counterintelligence organisations that respond to incursions on military installations, and the security review office that clears what its personnel may say in public. It is the institution against which the legacy programme allegation is principally made.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Department has controlled every official UAP investigation for seventy-nine years and, by its own inspector general's finding, still had no coordinated approach and no comprehensive response plan eighteen months after Congress ordered it to build one. Its structure gives it the two things a concealed recovery programme requires: an unacknowledged special access programme system whose existence need not be disclosed, and counterintelligence organisations designated as the first responders to any anomalous incursion on any installation or range. Congress has twice legislated as though it believes unreported UAP compartments exist, first by giving AARO statutory access notwithstanding all access controls, then by forbidding the expenditure of funds on UAP-related special access activity not reported to the intelligence committees. A former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council testified under oath that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies and that the effort is hidden from elected representatives. The Department's own Historical Record Report concedes that a controlled access compartment was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.
dossier.narrative:
The Department's UAP history is documented by its own inspector general. The first official DoD UAP activity was PROJECT SIGN, established by the Air Force Chief of Staff in December 1947. From 1947 to 1949 Air Force personnel investigated 243 reported sightings. In 1952 the Air Force Director of Intelligence initiated PROJECT BLUE BOOK, which investigated more than 12,000 sightings before its termination in 1969. Then, in the inspector general's own words, the DoD did not officially look at UAP again until mid-2000, when select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme to study UAP under the direction of the Defense Intelligence Agency. That sentence is worth pausing on. The Department's own watchdog records that the resumption of UAP work was not a Departmental decision at all. It was a congressional earmark inserted over the Department's disinterest, and when the Senate Majority Leader asked for it to be made a Special Access Program in June 2009 the Deputy Secretary of Defense declined on the advice of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

That forty-year gap is the load-bearing claim of the official account and the weakest point in it. The Department asks the public to accept that between BLUE BOOK's closure in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 it did nothing on the subject at all, in the same period in which it was operating an unacknowledged special access programme architecture whose whole purpose is that its contents cannot be inferred from budget documents or organisation charts.

Congress does not appear to accept it. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA forced the creation of an office. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the creation of a reporting mechanism usable notwithstanding non-disclosure agreements and free from reprisal. Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the historical report. Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA went further and prohibited the use of authorised funds for any special access or restricted access programme activity relating to UAP that has not been reported to the congressional committees by the Director of National Intelligence, and extended the restriction to contractor Independent Research and Development. Legislators do not write funding prohibitions against activities they believe do not exist.

The Deputy Secretary's July 2022 establishment memorandum is the Department's own consolidation instrument. It made AARO the authoritative office for all UAP and UAP-related activities, disestablished the Navy task force, and directed every DoD component holding UAP data, analysis, contracts or other material to synchronise immediately with AARO. If material and paperwork from a legacy programme existed anywhere in the Department, that memorandum is the order that would have moved it, and it moved it into an office reporting to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security.

The inspector general's evaluation, DODIG-2023-109, is the best independent measure of the Department's conduct. Its unclassified summary, released 24 January 2024, found that the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP; that DoD components had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands, the organisations actually responsible for detecting and preventing threats against the United States; that components had developed varying informal processes; and that the Department had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan. The evaluation notes that the Military Services and counterintelligence organisations had sent some UAP incident reports to AARO but that the Department does not formally require them to do so. It also records that the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report. That is three of the Department's most senior officials refusing to go on the record with the inspector general on this subject.

The response architecture matters as much as the analytic one. AARO's FY2025 report states that the military Services' counterintelligence, law enforcement and security agencies are the cognizant authorities responsible for responding to UAP incidents and incursions on all installations and ranges, and that AARO aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025. The doctrine governing what the United States military does when an anomalous object comes down on its property is classified, and the organisations that would execute it are Army Counterintelligence, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. Those are the same organisations that, in the concealment argument, would administer the silence.

Luis Elizondo, who told the House Oversight Committee in November 2024 that in his last government position he managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council, testified in writing that UAP are real, that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies, and that the country is in the midst of a multi-decade secretive arms race funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from elected representatives and oversight bodies. He testified that a small cadre within the government has created a culture of suppression and intimidation including unwarranted criminal investigations and harassment, and that the Pentagon's public affairs office employs a professional psychological operations officer as the single point of contact for UAP inquiries from citizens and the media.

The Department's posture since February 2026 has been transparency by executive channel. Secretary Hegseth committed to full compliance with a presidential disclosure directive, and a War Department official told DefenseScoop that AARO was working in close coordination with the White House to consolidate existing UAP records collections and facilitate the expeditious release of never-before-seen UAP information. The releases run through a departmental website rather than through the statutory National Archives collection, which puts the pace and the redactions back inside the Department.
