l0.label: National Aeronautics and Space Administration

dossier.whatItIs: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the U.S. civil space agency. Since 2022 it has been a formal participant in the government's UAP effort through a commissioned Independent Study Team, whose final report it published on 14 September 2023 alongside the appointment of a Director of UAP Research. Since 2026 it has been a contributing agency to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, supplying Apollo- and Gemini-era imagery and astronaut accounts.
dossier.whyImplicated: NASA's role in the concealment architecture is not custody; it is certification. It is the civilian, scientifically credentialed institution that repeatedly states there is no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while holding, by its own design choices, no access to the compartmented material where the question would actually be settled — its Independent Study Team used unclassified data only, and its charter expressly excluded review of past incidents. The sharper fact is a custody claim. In 2025 NASA's Office of Communications told a records researcher that it has no UAP records qualifying for transfer to the National Archives under the FY2024 NDAA because "any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That single sentence removes NASA's UAP holdings from the statutory records regime by attributing ownership to the department least likely to release them. Ten months later NASA's own Administrator publicly identified NASA-provided Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 lunar-surface imagery as "some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure." Both statements cannot sit comfortably together: an agency with nothing to transfer, holding the most interesting data.
dossier.narrative:
NASA entered the modern UAP file formally in 2022, when it commissioned an outside Independent Study Team to advise on how the agency might contribute. The team's final report was published on 14 September 2023 under NASA release 23-106, chaired by David Spergel, president of the Simons Foundation, with sixteen members. Its overall recommendation was that NASA play a prominent role in the whole-of-government effort by using its open-source resources, technological expertise, data analysis techniques, federal and commercial partnerships, and Earth-observing assets to curate a better dataset for understanding future UAP. The report explicitly is not a review or assessment of previous UAP incidents. That boundary is the point: NASA's charter for the study excluded the historical record, which is where the legacy program question lives.

Spergel described the methodological constraint as a virtue: "Using unclassified data was essential for our team's fact-finding, open-communication collaboration, and for upholding scientific rigor to produce this report for NASA." The team reported that there are currently a limited number of high-quality observations of UAP, which make it impossible to draw firm scientific conclusions about their nature. The same architecture reappears three years later in the UAP Science Advisory Council chaired by Avi Loeb — unclassified data only, chartered to recommend how to get better data, structurally incapable of reaching a custody finding. NASA built the template.

With the report NASA named Mark McInerney its Director of UAP Research. McInerney had previously served as NASA's liaison to the Department of Defense "covering limited UAP activities for the agency" — meaning the agency's UAP function had already existed as a DoD liaison billet before it was given a public title. Administrator Bill Nelson framed the role in terms of instrumentation and analytics: the director would apply "artificial intelligence and machine learning to search the skies for anomalies," and "NASA will do this work transparently for the benefit of humanity." McInerney's career runs through NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, NOAA and the National Hurricane Center since 1996 — a NOAA lineage he shares with Tim Gallaudet, the retired admiral now on the 2026 UAP Science Advisory Council.

Then came the records question, and with it the most consequential NASA statement in the public record. The FY2024 NDAA, sections 1841-1842, required federal agencies to identify and transfer UAP records to a new collection at the National Archives, with digital transfers due by 30 September 2025. Record Group 615 was created to hold them. Over the course of 2025 the FAA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the National Security Agency, ODNI and the Office of the Secretary of Defense transferred records into the online catalog. NASA did not. Asked why, NASA's Office of Communications replied: "Per the requirements in Section 1841-1842 of the Fiscal Year 2024 National Defense Authorization Act for handling records related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), NASA does not have any records that meet the requirements to submit records to the National Archives. Any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That is not a denial of possession. It is an assertion of foreign ownership over material NASA holds — a jurisdictional argument that keeps agency UAP records outside a statutory public-release regime by routing their custody back into the Department of War.

The 2026 disclosure wave then produced the contradiction. On 27 May 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that the newly declassified files show "real unexplained phenomena" but no recovered craft: "What's being surfaced isn't crashed ships or alien bodies, but real unexplained phenomena," and "There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships." Note the construction — personal awareness, from a political appointee without read-in to the compartments where such material would be held. In the same interview Isaacman said agencies "really didn't take this quite as seriously in the past until President Trump put out the tweet, basically giving an order to government agencies and going out and saying, look, this time you better go through the files, you better start searching your databases and bring things up" — a sitting NASA Administrator stating that federal agencies did not conduct records searches for UAP material until a presidential post compelled them.

And on NASA's own contribution: "I would say that some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure was taken on the surface of the moon from Apollo 12 and 17. You can't be a moon landing denier and also believe that those photos captured unexplained phenomenon." Fox News reported that the PURSUE material includes astronaut and NASA-related accounts from the Apollo and Gemini eras describing strange lights and unidentified objects observed in space, alongside 2023 infrared footage of an F-16 engaging a diamond-shaped object over Lake Huron and reports from military operations in Iran, Syria, Iraq and Greece. Set against the 2025 Office of Communications statement — NASA has no qualifying records because DoD owns them — the position is that NASA's most interesting UAP data was released through the Department of War's website rather than deposited in the National Archives collection Congress created for exactly that purpose. One route is statutory, permanent and indexed; the other is a rolling, discretionary web publication controlled by the Secretary of War. NASA's material went down the second.

A loose thread worth pulling: on the war.gov PURSUE page, the Release 05 slideshow of 7 August 2026 carries an image described as "A photograph of an unidentified object in low-Earth orbit, taken from Space Shuttle Columbia in 1996," while the underlying file is named DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953.jpg. A 1996 Columbia photograph filed under a 1953 film analysis is either a metadata error or an indexing artifact, and either way it is a checkable discrepancy in the government's own release. The Columbia 1996 imagery in question is almost certainly from STS-75, the tethered satellite mission whose downlink footage has been argued over for thirty years — meaning the 2026 disclosure has quietly placed a long-contested NASA video into an official unresolved-case release.

dossier.whatItIs: The Central Intelligence Agency is the United States civilian foreign intelligence service. Its documented involvement with the UFO question runs from the Office of Scientific Intelligence study group of 1952 through its convening of the Robertson Panel in January 1953 to its management of the U-2 and OXCART cover stories through the 1950s and 1960s. Its own in-house historian published a detailed account of that record in Studies in Intelligence in 1997.
dossier.whyImplicated: The CIA is the only agency in this dossier set that has published, in its own classified-origin journal, a first-person institutional admission that it directed the government to debunk UFO reports, concealed its sponsorship of the panel that recommended doing so, and knowingly allowed the Air Force to issue misleading and deceptive statements about more than half of all UFO reports for over a decade. That is not an allegation; it is the CIA's own historian describing the machinery of a UFO cover story and calling it by name. Once an agency has demonstrably run one UFO cover story for a real classified programme, the argument that it would not run a second for a different one loses its force. The Agency also sits at the point in the concealment argument where a recovery capability would have to live if the operations occurred on foreign soil, and it has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
dossier.narrative:
The primary document here is Gerald K. Haines, CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90, published in Studies in Intelligence in 1997 and posted on the Agency's own website. Haines was a government historian with access to Agency files. What he wrote is more damaging to the Agency's credibility on this subject than anything a critic has written.

The Robertson Panel convened in January 1953 at CIA's instigation, following a recommendation from the Intelligence Advisory Committee to enlist selected scientists to review and appraise the available evidence in light of pertinent scientific theories. The panellists had expertise in nuclear physics, high-energy physics, radar, electronics and geophysics. Their formal conclusion was that there was no evidence of a direct threat to national security and no evidence of extraterrestrial visitation. Their operational recommendation was something else entirely. Haines writes that to meet these problems, the panel recommended that the National Security Council debunk UFO reports and institute a policy of public education to reassure the public of the lack of evidence behind UFOs. It suggested using the mass media, advertising, business clubs, schools, and even the Disney corporation to get the message across. In the same breath, reporting at the height of McCarthyism, it recommended that private UFO groups including the Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators in Los Angeles and the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization be monitored for subversive activities.

That is a US intelligence agency recommending, at national security council level, a domestic public-opinion management campaign on a scientific subject and the surveillance of American civil society organisations that took an interest in it. The Agency then concealed its own role. When public pressure built for release of the panel report in 1956, Philip Strong, Deputy Assistant Director of the Office of Scientific Intelligence, refused to declassify it and declined to disclose CIA sponsorship of the panel. Haines records that the Agency instead prepared a sanitized version which deleted any reference to CIA and avoided mention of any psychological warfare potential in the UFO controversy. When Donald Keyhoe told Mike Wallace on CBS in March 1958 that the CIA was deeply involved and had sponsored the panel, the Agency held firm to its policy of not revealing its role in UFO investigations and refused to declassify the full report.

The U-2 passage is the strongest single piece of documentary evidence anywhere in the official record that the United States Government has deliberately generated false explanations for aerial phenomena and sustained them for years. Haines writes that Air Force BLUE BOOK investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights tried to explain away such sightings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and temperature inversions, that by checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in Washington they were able to attribute many UFO sightings to U-2 flights, and that they were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public. He then reports that according to later estimates from CIA officials who worked on the U-2 and OXCART projects, over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s were accounted for by manned reconnaissance flights, namely the U-2, over the United States, and that this led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily sensitive national security project. Haines adds that while perhaps justified, this deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup controversy of the 1970s.

The Agency also drafted, and then abandoned, a National Security Council Intelligence Directive on UFOs following the Robertson Panel findings. A directive of that class would have assigned standing intelligence community responsibility for the subject. That it was drafted at all establishes that the Agency treated UFOs as a candidate for permanent national intelligence tasking in 1953.

The modern allegations against the Agency are thinner and must be marked as such. Journalist Ross Coulthart has reported, on the basis of David Grusch and other sources, that an office within CIA has coordinated crash retrievals on foreign soil for many years. No document supporting that has been released, no named official has confirmed it on the record, and this board carries it at Tier 3 as a research direction rather than a finding. AARO's Volume I addresses a related allegation and reports that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which is an on-the-record denial obtained by an interested party rather than a document from the period.

What can be said cleanly is this. AARO states it partnered with CIA archives for the historical review, so the Agency's UAP holdings were at least nominally opened to the office writing the government's history. Yet as of 22 May 2026 the CIA does not appear among the seven organisations with a transmittal in the National Archives UAP Records Collection. Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, named the CIA first among the agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading in his words to unchecked power and corruption. An agency with a published institutional history of running UFO cover stories, no statutory records transmittal, and a named place in sworn whistleblower testimony belongs on this map.

l0.label: United States House of Representatives

dossier.whatItIs: The United States House of Representatives, and specifically the three bodies within it that have repeatedly touched the legacy program question: the Committee on Armed Services, which held the first open congressional UFO hearing in 1966; the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, which has run the modern public hearings since 2023; and that committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna. The House is also the chamber whose FY2024 NDAA conference product created the statutory UAP Records Collection at the National Archives.
dossier.whyImplicated: The House is not a bystander in this record; it is the institution that has been lied to, and periodically the institution that catches the lie. Its 1966 Armed Services hearing extracted the Air Force's official position on the record from a sitting Secretary and simultaneously put J. Allen Hynek's dissent into the Congressional record. Its Oversight Committee in 2023 put a former Navy pilot and other witnesses in front of cameras under oath. Its members have since gone after the contractor layer directly, issuing legislative interrogatories to The MITRE Corporation and MIT Lincoln Laboratory rather than to executive agencies, which is a deliberate move around the FOIA exemptions and classification authorities that block agency requests. And the House is where the funding lever sits: FY2024 NDAA section 1687 makes UAP-related independent research and development costs unallowable as indirect expenses unless the underlying material is made available to the defense and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership.
dossier.narrative:
The House's involvement runs on a sixty-year cycle of the same three moves: hearing, denial, statute.

Move one, 1966. On April 5, 1966 the Committee on Armed Services of the House of Representatives, 89th Congress, second session, held a hearing on Unidentified Flying Objects, convened after pressure from House Minority Leader Gerald Ford. The Air Force sent Secretary Harold Brown, and Project Blue Book sent Major Hector Quintanilla, its serving chief, and Dr. J. Allen Hynek, its scientific consultant. Brown put the Air Force position on the record: no evidence that UFOs threatened national security or were extraterrestrial. Hynek used the same hearing to place on the record that the Air Force's practice of assigning conventional explanations to every report was a poverty of hypotheses, and to call for an independent civilian scientific panel. The Air Force's response was to fund the Condon study at the University of Colorado, which is the template: a congressional hearing produces not disclosure but an outsourced study whose public summary can be written to a conclusion. That is exactly what had already been done with Battelle and Special Report No. 14 eleven years earlier.

Move two, 2023 to 2026. On July 26, 2023 the Oversight Committee's Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, chaired by Rep. Glenn Grothman with Rep. Robert Garcia as ranking member, and driven by Reps. Tim Burchett and Anna Paulina Luna, held the first public hearing to take testimony from military pilots and whistleblowers. Ryan Graves's written statement placed three institutional claims into the record: that UAP in U.S. airspace are grossly underreported; that stigma is itself a national security problem; and that excessive classification is hiding what the government knows, with all UAP video classified secret or above since 2021. Graves also entered a specific, dated, attributable account of information suppression: his advisor Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue' attaching the GO FAST video, and the following day the email was removed from Gallaudet's system and from his deputy's, with no one ever discussing it again. Gallaudet's own stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That single paragraph in a House witness statement is the cleanest documented instance of a UAP record being pulled out of an official system.

By 2025 the House had institutionalized the effort. Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets and named Luna to chair it, with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member and Republican members Nancy Mace, Tim Burchett, Lauren Boebert, Eric Burlison, Eli Crane and Brandon Gill, and Democratic members Stephen Lynch, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Dave Min. On September 9, 2025 the task force held a hearing on restoring public trust through UAP transparency and whistleblower protection, taking testimony from Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland.

Move three, statute. The FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, sections 1841 through 1843, directed NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and required every federal agency to review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by October 20, 2024. The statutory definition of what belongs in the collection is the tell: copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence. Congress wrote non-human intelligence into a records statute. NARA's implementing metadata schema then required a mandatory Special Controls field populated with SAP, SCI, RD/FRD and FGI markings, and required the Department of Energy to be entered as a referral agency whenever a file contains Restricted Data or Formerly Restricted Data. The Archives built its intake to receive special-access and nuclear-classified UAP material before anyone had produced any. Separately, section 1687(b) of the same law made UAP-related independent research and development funding unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and the four congressional leaders. That provision exists because someone in Congress concluded that contractors were charging the taxpayer for UAP work through overhead while reporting nothing.

By 2026 the House had pivoted to attacking the contractor and FFRDC layer directly. Burlison's May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE, and his earlier letter to MIT Lincoln Laboratory, assert that a nonprofit FFRDC cannot become a private vault for federal records. On August 1, 2026 Burlison released, with administration authorization, preliminary implementation guidance for President Trump's directive on nondisclosure agreements binding current and former government employees and contractors with UAP information, and invited anyone who believes the directive applies to them to contact his office. That is a sitting member of the House offering himself as the intake channel for people whose NDAs may have just been waived. Running alongside it, and not through it, the administration began posting declassified interagency UAP files in May 2026 on war.gov/ufo, an executive release track that answers to no congressional deadline.

Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 (Dec. 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 621) provides that independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena 'shall not be allowable as indirect expenses' for covered contracts under DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless such material and information is made available to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.

Rep. Eric Burlison, a member of both the Oversight Committee and the Task Force, transmitted legislative interrogatories to The MITRE Corporation on May 22, 2026 and had previously sent a records demand to MIT Lincoln Laboratory concerning the Beacon Hill Study and the recording 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52'.

On August 1, 2026 Rep. Burlison publicly released, with administration authorization, preliminary implementation guidance for President Trump's directive on nondisclosure agreements covering current and former government employees and contractors with UAP-related information, following his July 21, 2026 statement inviting affected individuals to contact his office.

The Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 (118th Congress), introduced by the Chairman and Ranking Member of the House Oversight National Security Subcommittee, would allow civilian pilots to report UAP through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System, provide protection against retaliation, and make all UAP reports publicly available.

In May 2026 the administration began posting declassified interagency UAP files as part of President Trump's disclosure initiative, with the first tranche published on war.gov/ufo, an executive-branch release running parallel to, rather than through, the congressional records process.

dossier.denialPosture: The House does not deny; it is the venue in which denials are entered. l0.label: Information Security Oversight Office

dossier.whatItIs: The Information Security Oversight Office, a component of the National Archives and Records Administration, established by Section 5.2 of Executive Order 13526 to develop implementing directives for the national security classification system, oversee agency compliance, and report at least annually to the President. Its Director is appointed by the Archivist of the United States subject to the approval of the President; the current Director is Michael D. Thomas, successor to Mark A. Bradley. ISOO is, on paper, the only government-wide civilian oversight body for classified information.
dossier.whyImplicated: ISOO is implicated by absence, not by action. In fifty years of annual reports to the President, ISOO has never reported the existence of a program engaged in the recovery or exploitation of non-human craft — and the reason is that the Executive Order that created ISOO also built the trapdoor through which such a program would fall. Section 4.3(b)(3) of E.O. 13526 says the ISOO Director 'shall be afforded access' to special access programs, then immediately permits an agency head to limit that access to the Director plus one employee, or, for programs deemed 'extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable,' to the Director alone. Section 5.2(b)(4) goes further: an agency head who believes ISOO access would pose 'an exceptional national security risk' may recommend denial to the President through the National Security Advisor, and 'Access shall be denied pending the response.' The denial is self-executing. ISOO's oversight is therefore contingent on the consent of the agency being overseen. Every ISOO annual report is an accounting of the classification system that a concealed waived SAP would not appear in, and ISOO would not know it was missing.
dossier.narrative:
ISOO is the institution people point to when they say the classification system has oversight. Read the authorities and the picture inverts: ISOO is the institution that documents the boundary of what oversight cannot see.

The charter is Executive Order 13526, signed 29 December 2009. Section 5.2(a) places ISOO inside the National Archives and gives the Archivist the appointment power over its Director, subject to presidential approval. Section 5.2(b) lists nine functions: develop directives, oversee agency compliance, approve agency implementing regulations, conduct on-site reviews, review requests for original classification authority, take action on complaints, standardize forms, report annually to the President, and chair interagency meetings. Section 5.1(a) makes ISOO directives 'binding on the agencies.' On its face this is real authority.

Then come the carve-outs, and they are written with unusual care.

Section 5.2(b)(4) grants ISOO the authority to conduct on-site reviews of any agency program 'and to require of each agency those reports and information and other cooperation that may be necessary to fulfill its responsibilities.' The very next sentence is the trapdoor: 'If granting access to specific categories of classified information would pose an exceptional national security risk, the affected agency head or the senior agency official shall submit a written justification recommending the denial of access to the President through the National Security Advisor within 60 days of the request for access. Access shall be denied pending the response.' An agency head who wants to keep ISOO out of a compartment does not need to win an argument. He needs to file a paper and wait. Access is denied by default during the pendency, and the order sets no deadline for the President to respond.

Section 4.3 is where the structure becomes specific to special access programs. Only six officials may create a SAP — the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each. Section 4.3(b)(2) requires each agency head to 'establish and maintain a system of accounting for special access programs' — note that the accounting system is the agency's, not ISOO's. Section 4.3(b)(3) provides ISOO access, then caps it: 'An agency head may limit access to a special access program to the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.' A single human being, with no staff, no analysts, and no ability to delegate, is the entire oversight footprint for the most sensitive category of American secrecy.

And then Section 4.3(c), one sentence, easy to skip: 'Nothing in this order shall supersede any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119.' Section 119 of Title 10 is the congressional SAP oversight statute. It requires annual reports to the defense committees identifying each SAP, its cost history, and its milestones — and subsection (e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content requirement 'if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security,' delivering the information instead only 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' That is the statutory birth certificate of the waived SAP: a program known to four members of Congress and to no one else on the Hill. E.O. 13526 does not disturb it.

The oversight picture then gets worse, not better. The Office of Law Revision Counsel's note to 10 U.S.C. 119 records that the annual reporting requirements in subsections (a) and (b) — the SAP inventory and the new-program notification — were terminated effective 31 December 2021 by Section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The one recurring, statutory, cross-committee accounting of DoD special access programs sunset four years ago, in the same window in which Congress was writing UAP oversight law on the assumption that unreported restricted-access programs existed.

So the analytical position is this. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort is carried as a waived unacknowledged SAP or under a non-DoD authority such as an Atomic Energy Act restricted-data compartment, ISOO would have no independent way to detect it. It has no access it cannot be denied, no staff it can bring, no inventory it maintains itself, and no statutory partner report to cross-check against since 2021. ISOO's annual report to the President — the FY2024 edition was transmitted in early August 2025 and publicly issued on 18 September 2025 by Director Michael D. Thomas, the first of his tenure, restructured around four areas of action — is an honest accounting of the classification system as agencies choose to describe it to ISOO.

That is the argument. ISOO is not a participant in concealment. ISOO is the measuring instrument that was built with a blind spot exactly the shape of the thing being hidden, and the blind spot was written into the order by the same executive branch that would be operating in it.

claims.text: The Information Security Oversight Office is established within the National Archives by Section 5.2(a) of Executive Order 13526, and its Director is appointed by the Archivist of the United States subject to the approval of the President.

E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(b)(3) permits an agency head to limit ISOO's access to a special access program to 'the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.'

E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.2(b)(4) provides that where an agency head recommends denial of ISOO access on grounds of 'exceptional national security risk,' the written justification goes to the President through the National Security Advisor within 60 days and 'Access shall be denied pending the response.'
Under E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(b)(2), the system of accounting for special access programs is maintained by each agency head, not by ISOO.

Only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program absent separate presidential authorization.

E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(c) states in full: 'Nothing in this order shall supersede any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119,' preserving the statutory SAP reporting regime and its waiver mechanism intact against the classification order.

10 U.S.C. 119(e) authorizes the Secretary of Defense to waive, case by case, any requirement that specified information be included in a SAP report to the defense committees where inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' and to provide that information and the waiver justification only 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

The annual SAP reporting requirements in 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) were terminated effective 31 December 2021 by Section 1061 of Public Law 114-328, eliminating the recurring statutory inventory of DoD special access programs delivered to the defense committees.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) bars initiation of a special access program until the defense committees are notified and 30 days elapse — a notification requirement that survives the 2021 termination of the annual reports.

ISOO directives issued under E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.1(a) are 'binding on the agencies,' and Sec. 5.2(b)(8) requires the Director to report at least annually to the President on implementation of the order.

ISOO transmitted its Fiscal Year 2024 Annual Report to the President in early August 2025 and publicly issued it on 18 September 2025; it was the first annual report of Director Michael D. Thomas's tenure and restructured ISOO's mission into four areas: Oversight and Compliance, Guidance and Implementation, Data Collection and Analysis, and Administration and Engagement.

ISOO's published annual reports run back to 1979, providing a continuous forty-five-year government-wide accounting of the classification system in which no recovery or exploitation program for non-human technology has been reported.
claims.source: https://www.archives.gov/isoo/reports/annual-report-archive.html ; see also https://isoo-overview.blogs.archives.gov/2025/09/18/announcing-the-publication-of-isoos-fiscal-year-2024-annual-report-to-the-president/ ('I studied our prior releases, dating all the way back to 1979')

claims.text: Under E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.2(b)(6), ISOO is required to 'consider and take action on complaints and suggestions from persons within or outside the Government' regarding administration of the classification program, providing a standing external channel that has not, on the public record, produced a UAP-related classification finding.

ISOO sits inside the same agency, NARA, that the FY2024 NDAA designated as custodian of the UAP Records Collection and that the FY2027 Burlison amendment would make the permanent home of that collection.

dossier.denialPosture: ISOO does not deny the existence of a legacy program; it has never made an affirmative public statement on the subject either way. Its posture is structural silence — an annual report to the President that accounts for the classification system as agencies self-report it, produced by an office that E.O. 13526 permits any of six agency heads to lock out of the relevant compartment with a single memorandum to the National Security Advisor.
connections: Michael D. Thomas, current ISOO Director, signatory of the FY2024 Annual Report to the President; predecessor Mark A. Bradley.
Reports through the Archivist of the United States, who is also the statutory custodian of the UAP Records Collection under the FY2024 NDAA and under the Burlison FY2027 amendment.

Directly linked to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security and the DoD Special Access Program Central Office (SAPCO), which run the DoD SAP accounting system that E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(b)(2) leaves in agency hands.

The 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver channel routes SAP information to four individuals — the chairman and ranking member of the House and Senate Armed Services and Appropriations committees — which is the same narrow channel referenced in 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(A) as the test for whether a program has been 'explicitly and clearly reported' to Congress.

Chairs the National Industrial Security Program Policy Advisory Committee (NISPPAC), the contractor-facing side of the classification system and therefore the interface with the prime contractors named in reverse-engineering testimony.

The Director serves as Executive Secretary of the Interagency Security Classification Appeals Panel (ISCAP) under E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.3(a)(4), the only body that can override an agency declassification denial.
openQuestions: How many times, if ever, has an agency head invoked the E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.2(b)(4) denial-of-access procedure against ISOO, and for which compartments? No public accounting of these filings has been identified.

Whether ISOO's SAP oversight under Sec. 4.3(b)(3) has ever been exercised against a waived unacknowledged SAP, and whether any ISOO Director has ever been the single authorized reader of such a program.
Whether the FY2024 or any prior ISOO annual report contains a count of special access programs across government; the reports were not read in full for this dossier.
What replaced the terminated 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) annual reports after 31 December 2021, if anything, and whether the defense committees receive any equivalent inventory today.
Whether ISOO has any role in reviewing classification decisions applied to records transmitted to the NARA UAP Records Collection, or whether that review sits entirely with originating agencies.
Whether restricted data compartments under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 — which sit outside E.O. 13526's classification system entirely — are within ISOO's reach at all.
Whether any ISOO Director has been briefed on a UAP-related program and, if so, whether that briefing appears in any ISOO record.

l0.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)

dossier.whatItIs: The classified addenda -- variously called annexes, schedules, appendices and supplements -- attached to the three annual national security statutes (Intelligence Authorization Act, National Defense Authorization Act, Department of Defense Appropriations Act) and to the committee reports that accompany them. Together with the classified notification channels of 10 U.S.C. 119, they are the legal machinery by which Congress appropriates money and issues binding direction to programs whose existence is not public. No classified annex has ever been published, in any form, redacted or otherwise.
dossier.whyImplicated: If a legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering effort has been funded for eight decades, the money moved through this channel, because there is no other channel that both carries the force of law and never surfaces. The annex system is not a leak in oversight; it is a purpose-built container that gives classified direction "the legal status of public law" while keeping it in a safe in a secure room that few members ever enter. Layered on top of it, 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense strip specified content out of the Special Access Program reports entirely and deliver it to only eight people -- the chair and ranking member of four committees. And the statutory backbone that forced annual SAP disclosure at all, 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b), was terminated effective December 31, 2021 by a sunset provision Congress itself enacted. David Grusch's sworn answer to the funding question -- "misappropriation of funds and self-fund" -- describes an abuse that this architecture is uniquely well designed to conceal, because the annex records what Congress intended to buy but the public record cannot be reconciled against it.
dossier.narrative:
The classified annex is the least glamorous object on this board and the most important. It is the mechanism that makes the rest of the question -- who, where, under what authority, paid for how -- answerable in principle and unanswerable in practice.

Dakota Rudesill, a former Senate Budget Committee staffer and Intelligence Community official, published the only serious empirical study of the practice. His finding: over thirty-six years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda the force of law, and produced at least 271 committee reports carrying classified addenda since 1977. About half of the 124 were incorporation provisions -- statutory text whose entire operative content is a pointer to a document nobody outside the compartment will ever see. The standard formulation appears at Section 102 of virtually every Intelligence Authorization Act: the amounts authorized and the personnel ceilings "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations." Accompanying report language routinely states that the Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law." The Intelligence Community's own top lawyer has agreed with that characterization.

Rudesill is careful, and his carefulness is itself evidence. He notes that nothing is publicly known about the length of any annex -- "An individual addendum could be two pages long, or 20, or 200" -- and that each committee invites members to read the addenda in a secure room, but "few do." He also records that the practice accelerated: Congress wrote more force-of-law annex provisions in 2011-2015 than in the first eight Congresses of the practice combined, from 1977 to 1992. This is the shape of a mechanism that grew because it worked.

The second layer is statutory rather than procedural. 10 U.S.C. 119 is the SAP oversight statute. Subsection (a) requires an annual March 1 report to the four defense committees listing every DoD special access program, with descriptions, milestones, actual costs by year, and estimated costs across a six-year horizon. Subsection (b) requires a February 1 notice and justification for every new SAP. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. On its face this is real oversight.

Subsection (e) is the escape hatch. The Secretary of Defense "may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report" upon determining that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security." When he does, the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- eight members of Congress, no staff specified. DoD Instruction 5205.11 builds the corresponding category into doctrine: a waived SAP is "An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

The third layer is the one almost nobody has noticed. The U.S. Code note appended to Section 119 reads: "For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328." The annual SAP report and the new-SAP notice -- the two provisions that produced a written, dated, comprehensive inventory of the black budget's program structure -- were swept away by a generic reporting-burden sunset enacted in the FY2017 NDAA. The subsection (e) waiver survives; the reports it was designed to abridge do not.

Against that background, Congress in December 2022 legislated a tell. 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) -- Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA -- requires the Secretary of Defense, within 72 hours, to report to the defense and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership any authorized UAP disclosure that relates to "a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees." Congress does not write 72-hour tripwires for hypotheticals. The statute is a signed, dated legislative acknowledgment that unreported access programs are a live possibility.

AARO has since conceded, in its own words, one instance: "In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering." AARO adds that the program never recovered or reverse-engineered anything and was disestablished for lack of merit. Set aside the exculpatory half. The admitted half is that a controlled access program was expanded without sufficient justification, in 2021, specifically to protect UAP reverse-engineering -- which is precisely the nesting behavior Grusch described when he said agencies were "nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities."

Finally, the annex logic reappears in the disclosure statute itself. Under Section 1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, a UAP record may be withheld from the National Archives collection when "the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence" of enumerated harms. The original classification authority is the agency holding the record. The annex principle -- the withholder judges the withholding -- survived into the law written to end it.

claims.text: Congress attaches classified addenda to three annual national security acts -- the Intelligence Authorization Act, the National Defense Authorization Act, and the Department of Defense Appropriations Act -- and no addendum has ever been published, even in redacted form.
claims.source: Dakota S. Rudesill, "Classified Legislation: Tracking Congress's Library of Secret Law," Lawfare, May 19, 2016, https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/classified-legislation-tracking-congresss-library-secret-law

claims.text: Over 36 years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda legal force; about half were full or partial incorporation provisions. Counting committee reports, Congress has produced at least 271 reports with classified addenda since 1977.

Virtually all annual Intelligence Authorization Acts stipulate at Section 102 that funding authorizations and personnel levels "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations," and accompanying report language states that the classified Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law."

Congress has used annex-incorporation provisions to earmark specific sums invisibly, including $4.8 billion for "classified programs, described...in the classified annex" at the height of the Iraq war.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive any requirement under subsections (a), (b) or (c) that certain information be included in a special access program report if the Secretary determines that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security," on a case-by-case basis.

When the Secretary of Defense exercises the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver, the withheld information and the waiver justification go only "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- eight members of Congress.

The annual DoD special access program report (10 U.S.C. 119(a)) and the annual new-SAP notice and justification (10 U.S.C. 119(b)) were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328, the FY2017 NDAA.

An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

AARO's own historical review states: "In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering. This program never recovered or reverse-engineered any UAP or extraterrestrial spacecraft. This IC program was disestablished due to its lack of merit."

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue here, because the mechanism is openly documented in statute and doctrine and defended on its merits: the Intelligence Community's chief lawyer has publicly agreed that classified schedules carry the legal status of public law. The concealment is not denied; it is legislated.
connections: 10 U.S.C. 119 is the statutory hinge shared with dodi-5205-11: DoDI 5205.11 implements Section 119, and its 'waived SAP' category exists only because Section 119(e) authorizes the waiver.

Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA (50 U.S.C. 3373b), drafted with input from David Grusch while he was in government, created the 72-hour tripwire for programs not reported to the defense or intelligence committees -- the direct legislative counterpart to grusch-misappropriation-allegation.
Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA (nara-rg615) transplant the annex logic into the disclosure regime by leaving postponement to the original classification authority.

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer's UAP Disclosure Amendment, quoted at the July 26, 2023 hearing for the phrase 'technologies of unknown origins, non-human intelligence, and unexplainable phenomena,' was the legislative attempt to break the annex model.
AARO's admitted 2021 expansion of an IC Controlled Access Program 'to protect UAP reverse-engineering' links this mechanism directly to manhattan-project-2 and to the AAWSAP/AATIP-KONA BLUE lineage.

Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, arranged the first congressional staff briefings on retrievals (Senate Armed Services staff, October 21, 2019; Senate Intelligence staff two days later), working the same committee channel the annexes flow through.
openQuestions: Whether any classified annex from 1944 to the present contains a line item, program identifier or nickname corresponding to a materials-retrieval or exploitation effort -- no annex has ever been released.
Which specific SAPs, if any, have had 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waivers applied to them, and how many waivers have been issued in total; the statute requires no public accounting.
Whether the December 31, 2021 termination of the 119(a) and 119(b) reporting requirements was substantively debated or was a drafting artifact of a generic reporting-burden sunset.
Whether the DoD or IC has ever complied with the 72-hour notification requirement of 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B), and how many such notifications have been made.
The identity of the IC Controlled Access Program whose scope AARO says was expanded in 2021 'without sufficient justification' to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and who authorized the expansion.

l0.label: The misappropriation allegation: Grusch's ICIG complaint and sworn testimony

dossier.whatItIs: A protected whistleblower complaint and subsequent sworn congressional testimony by David Charles Grusch, a former Air Force officer, National Reconnaissance Office senior intelligence officer and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency co-lead for UAP analysis, alleging that a multi-decade U.S. crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering program exists, is concealed from Congress, and is sustained by the misappropriation of appropriated funds. The complaint was filed with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022 by Charles McCullough III, the first Senate-confirmed ICIG.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only allegation of its kind that has passed through a statutory inspector-general channel, been assessed as credible and urgent, been transmitted to the Director of National Intelligence and both intelligence committees, and then been repeated under oath in open session with the penalty of perjury attached. The specific charge is not that craft exist; it is a financial-crimes charge -- that money appropriated by Congress for other purposes was diverted, and that the diversion was the concealment method. That reframes the question from metaphysics to auditability. Grusch's counsel is the man who built the ICIG whistleblower system, which means the filing was engineered to survive procedurally. And Grusch's own hand appears in the FY2023 NDAA UAP language, so the statutory tripwires now on the books were drafted by the complainant against the mechanism he was complaining about.
dossier.narrative:
Precision matters more here than anywhere else on the board, because the allegation has been repeatedly restated in forms Grusch never used.

What he filed: in May 2022, Charles McCullough III -- senior partner at Compass Rose Legal Group, and the original Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, confirmed by the Senate in 2011 under DNI James Clapper -- filed on Grusch's behalf a "Disclosure of Urgent Concern(s); Complaint of Reprisal" with the ICIG. The complaint concerned information Grusch had gathered beginning in 2019 while working with the UAP Task Force. All testimony Grusch provided for the classified complaint was given under oath, and the document closed with his signed affirmation: "I do solemnly affirm under the penalties of perjury that the contents of the foregoing paper are true and correct to the best of my knowledge."

What the unclassified version of the complaint says: that Grusch has direct knowledge that UAP-related classified information has been withheld and concealed from Congress by "elements" of the intelligence community "to purposely and intentionally thwart legitimate Congressional oversight of the UAP Program." Note the construction -- withheld from Congress, intentionally, to defeat oversight. That is an allegation about a crime against the legislature, not about biology.

What the ICIG did: found the complaint "credible and urgent" in July 2022. This is a procedural determination under the urgent-concern statute -- it means the complaint met the threshold for transmission, not that its substance was adjudicated true. Per Grusch, a summary went immediately to DNI Avril Haines, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. A whistleblower reprisal investigation was opened. Several current members of the alleged recovery program spoke to the Inspector General's office and, per reporting, corroborated information Grusch had provided.

What he said under oath on July 26, 2023, before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs. The core sentence: "I was informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program to which I was denied access to those additional read-ons when I requested it." Two things are asserted and one is not. Asserted: that he was officially informed such a program exists, and that he formally requested and was denied read-on. Not asserted: that he saw craft, materials or bodies himself. Every subsequent claim of first-hand observation attributed to him is a media artifact.

On funding, Representative Jared Moskowitz asked directly. Grusch: "I will give you generalities. I can get very specific in a closed session. But misappropriation of funds and self-fund." Two mechanisms, not one. Misappropriation -- money appropriated for a stated purpose spent on another. Self-fund -- the effort generating its own revenue, presumably through the commercial exploitation of derived technology, which would place private contractors inside the financial architecture rather than merely adjacent to it.

On sourcing, asked whether he had met people with direct knowledge of non-human origin craft, he answered: "Yes. I personally interviewed those individuals." On timeline, asked when contact first occurred: "I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's." On the campaign against public knowledge, in response to Representative Anna Paulina Luna, he referred to "a multi-decade, you know, campaign to disenfranchise public interest."

His pre-hearing DOPSR-cleared statements go further on the contracting angle: "Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia." He also characterized the effort as a "publicly unknown Cold War for recovered and exploited physical material -- a competition with near-peer adversaries over the years to identify UAP crashes/landings and retrieve the material for exploitation/reverse engineering to garner asymmetric national defense advantages."

The corroboration that matters is Karl E. Nell's, because Nell put his name to it while identifying himself by his official role. Nell, the Army's liaison to the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, said: "His assertion concerning the existence of a terrestrial arms race occurring sub-rosa over the past eighty years focused on reverse engineering technologies of unknown origin is fundamentally correct, as is the indisputable realization that at least some of these technologies of unknown origin derive from non-human intelligence." Nell also called Grusch "beyond reproach."

The institutional counter-position arrived in 2024. AARO's historical review concluded: "AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology," and attributed the narrative "in large part" to "circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case." AARO further asserts that "all the authentic programs have been properly notified and reported to Congress through the congressional defense and/or intelligence committees." That last sentence is a testable claim, and it is testable only against the classified annex.

As of 2026 the legal obstacle Grusch cited has formally been removed. On July 31, 2026, Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas issued memorandum ES 2026-00818 directing that prior nondisclosure agreements, oaths and commitments are waived for current and former employees and contractors speaking to AARO or to the PURSUE Task Force. The corroboration Grusch said existed in closed session is now, on paper, free to speak.

Asked whether he had met people with direct knowledge of non-human origin craft, Grusch testified: "Yes. I personally interviewed those individuals." He did not testify to first-hand observation of craft or materials.

Asked when U.S. contact with non-human intelligence first occurred, Grusch testified: "I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's."

In statements cleared for open publication by the DoD Office of Prepublication and Security Review on April 4 and 6, 2023, Grusch alleged "illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia."

Grusch served as the National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAP Task Force from 2019 to 2021 and as the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency's co-lead for UAP analysis and task force representative from late 2021 to July 2022, as a GS-15 cleared at TS/SCI; he left government on April 7, 2023.

Grusch helped draft the UAP language in the FY2023 National Defense Authorization Act, spearheaded by Senators Kirsten Gillibrand and Marco Rubio and signed into law in December 2022 -- the provisions now codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373b.

Retired Army Colonel Karl E. Nell, the Army's liaison to the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, stated on the record: "His assertion concerning the existence of a terrestrial arms race occurring sub-rosa over the past eighty years focused on reverse engineering technologies of unknown origin is fundamentally correct, as is the indisputable realization that at least some of these technologies of unknown origin derive from non-human intelligence."

50 U.S.C. 3373b(b)(1)(A) provides that an authorized disclosure "shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure," and 3373b(b)(2)(A) prohibits reprisal including revocation or suspension of security clearances.
