dossier.denialPosture: Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough stated that the Department had not discovered "any verifiable information to substantiate claims that any programs regarding the possession or reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial materials have existed in the past or exist currently," and separately that it had "no information that any individual has been harmed or killed as a result of providing information." AARO's 2024 historical review states it "found no empirical evidence" for reverse-engineering claims and attributes them to "circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case." Both are dated, attributable statements from institutions Grusch named as concealing; neither addresses the misappropriation-of-funds charge on its own terms.
connections: Charles McCullough III designed and ran the ICIG whistleblower channel he later used on Grusch's behalf -- the complainant's counsel is the architect of the mechanism.
Karl E. Nell corroborated Grusch on the record and appears again in manhattan-project-2 as the proponent of a state-scale reverse-engineering effort.

Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, said he had received detailed information from well-placed officials about the alleged program including 'the history, governing documents and the location where a craft was allegedly abandoned and recovered.'

Jonathan Grey of the National Air and Space Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson AFB went on the record in the same June 5, 2023 report asserting the existence of 'complex historical programs involving the coordinated retrieval and study of exotic materials, dating back to the early 20th century.'
The funding mechanism Grusch alleges is the one described in classified-annex; the program-structure mechanism is the one described in dodi-5205-11.
AARO's KONA BLUE disclosure is the Department's competing origin story for the same allegation set, tracing it to AAWSAP/AATIP, DIA and Bigelow Aerospace rather than to a legacy program.

Senators Kirsten Gillibrand and Marco Rubio sponsored the FY2023 NDAA UAP provisions Grusch helped draft; Reps. Tim Burchett, Anna Paulina Luna, Jared Moskowitz, Nancy Mace and Eric Burlison questioned him at the July 26, 2023 hearing.
openQuestions: Which appropriations accounts Grusch alleges were raided, and in what amounts -- he said he could 'get very specific in a closed session' and no unclassified specificity has followed.
What 'self-fund' means operationally: whether it denotes commercial revenue from derived technology, contractor cost-recovery, or something else.
Whether the ICIG reprisal investigation opened after July 2022 was ever completed, and what it found.
The identities of the more than forty individuals Grusch says he interviewed, and whether any have testified in closed session.
Whether the corroborating current members of the alleged program who spoke to the ICIG's office have been re-interviewed under the 2026 NDA waiver regime.
Whether AARO's assertion that 'all the authentic programs have been properly notified and reported to Congress' has ever been independently verified against the classified schedules.

l0.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region (DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00)
l0.short: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region

dossier.whatItIs: Project Condign was a classified UK Ministry of Defence study of unidentified aerial phenomena carried out for the Defence Intelligence Staff between 1996 and 2000, resulting in a three-volume, roughly 460-page report titled 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region.' It drew on approximately 10,000 UK sighting reports held by DI55, the Defence Intelligence branch responsible for UFO investigations inside the Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence. Classified 'Secret UK Eyes Only,' it was released in May 2006 after a Freedom of Information Act request by researchers David Clarke and Gary Anthony.
dossier.whyImplicated: Condign is the clearest documented case of a NATO partner's intelligence service running a multi-year, compartmented UAP program while telling the public and Parliament almost nothing. Its debunking conclusion sits alongside an explicit recommendation that the plasma phenomenon it invoked be examined for 'novel military applications,' with the implications already briefed to MoD technology managers — a technology-exploitation tasking hiding inside a dismissal document. Most importantly, the sections the MoD fought hardest to keep censored for two decades turned out not to concern aliens at all but rumoured US black programs (Aurora/Astra and the TR-3A 'Black Manta'), and the MoD's stated justification in February 2026 was that release 'could still provide adversaries with an insight into the developments of US/UK aircraft technology.' That is a government stating on the record that UAP files are classified in order to protect black aerospace programs, and doing so on behalf of a foreign partner. Condign also contains a precise, dated, attributable negative that any retrieval hypothesis has to answer: that no artefacts of unknown origin had ever been handed to UK authorities.
dossier.narrative:
Project Condign is the UK's answer to the question of what an intelligence service actually does with a national UFO file when it thinks nobody is watching. The MoD had, since the 1950s, maintained a nominal UFO desk that handled public correspondence. Behind it sat DI55, a section of the Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence within the Defence Intelligence Staff, which quietly collected sighting reports for defence-intelligence purposes. In 1996 DI55 commissioned defence scientist Ron Haddow — whom, according to David Clarke, DI55 regarded as their subject expert — to write a comprehensive assessment. Haddow was given access to the retained MoD holdings, worked for four years, and delivered in 2000 a three-volume study running to roughly 460 pages. It was classified Secret UK Eyes Only and, by Clarke's account, shown to only a handful of people.

The report's public reputation is as a debunking. That is a fair reading of its headline conclusions: 'There is no evidence that any UAP, seen in the UKADR, are incursions by air-objects of any intelligent (extra-terrestrial or foreign) origin, or that they represent any hostile intent,' and 'No artefacts of unknown or unexplained origin have been reported or handed to the UK authorities, despite thousands of UAP reports. There are no SIGINT, ELINT or radiation measurements and little useful video or still IMINT.' Those are unusually specific negatives, and they are the strongest single piece of counter-evidence a British-side retrieval narrative has to overcome. An honest board records them as such.

But the report is not only a debunking, and this is where it becomes load-bearing for the program argument. Its residual-explanation hypothesis is 'Buoyant Plasma Formation' — an atmospheric plasma phenomenon it proposes as the cause of black-triangle reports and of close-encounter perceptual effects, via electromagnetic fields that could 'adversely affect a vehicle or person.' Having proposed it, the report does not stop at explanation. It recommends further research into novel military applications of the phenomenon and records that 'the implications have already been briefed to the relevant MoD technology managers.' It also notes that scientists in the former Soviet Union had 'identified the close connection between the UFO Phenomena and Plasma technologies' and were 'pursuing related techniques for potential military purposes.' In other words: a classified UAP study concluding there is nothing to see also concluded that there was something worth weaponising, and routed it to acquisition people. That is the structural signature of an exploitation channel, and it is on the record in an executive summary the MoD itself released.

The second thread is the redactions. When Clarke received the report in 2006 — handed to him in MoD Main Building by Linda Unwin, then the penultimate UFO desk officer, a post abolished in 2009 — sections of volume 2 stamped NATO Secret were withheld. The MoD held that line for two decades through repeated FOI requests, invoking FOIA exemptions 24 (national security) and 27 (international relations), and as recently as February 2026 refused release on the grounds that disclosure 'could still provide adversaries with an insight into the developments of US/UK aircraft technology, compromising the military capabilities of US partners and our own Air Force assets.' Four months later the identical material was released in full to an anonymous requester. What it contained were two speculative paragraphs on the rumoured Aurora/Astra programme and on the TR-3A 'Black Manta,' with a figure annotating the latter as having a 60-foot wingspan and 42-foot length, described as 'covert survivable in weather strike/recce,' in two variants, one 'seen with sausage-shaped contrail (or smoke?)' and one 'probably/possibly with pulsating motor.' Also withheld had been head-on silhouettes of the F-117 and B-2 with the observation that their fuselage shapes 'can be reported respectively as saucer or arc/boomerang shaped under certain silhouette and lighting conditions,' and the note that 'these aircraft types are unfamiliar as they are rarely spotted in UK airspace.'

The analytic yield is twofold. First, the UK's defence intelligence establishment in the 1990s privately believed the Americans were flying triangular and diamond-shaped stealth platforms through UK airspace, with or without permission, and used that belief as an explanatory bin for domestic UAP reports — the same move AARO makes today. Second, the twenty-year classification of that material demonstrates the mechanism the board is trying to characterise: UAP secrecy sustained not because of what UAP are, but because black-program equities, including a partner nation's, attach to the same file. Clarke's own judgment on the 2006 release was that it shed no new light on the phenomenon but did show DIS had been running a far larger investigation than it had ever admitted.

What the record does not show is any Condign statement about materials, retrievals, or reverse-engineering — it explicitly denies artefacts. It says nothing about US programs beyond the Aurora and TR-3 speculation. And because the study was never peer reviewed, the plasma hypothesis has been challenged as one that would not have survived independent scrutiny.

claims.text: Project Condign was a Defence Intelligence Staff study conducted between 1996 and 2000, producing a report titled 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region' drawing on approximately 10,000 sightings gathered by DI55, a section of the Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence.

The report was released into the public domain on 15 May 2006 following a September 2005 Freedom of Information Act request by David Clarke of Sheffield Hallam University and Gary Anthony, a former BUFORA astronomical consultant.

David Clarke states that defence scientist Ron Haddow was commissioned in 1996 to write the report because DI55 regarded him as their expert on the subject, that the completed report was classified 'Secret UK Eyes Only,' and that his copy was handed to him in MoD Main Building by Linda Unwin, then the penultimate UFO desk officer, a post abolished in 2009.
The full report covers three volumes totalling 460 pages and uses the term UAP (Unidentified Aerial Phenomena) throughout in place of UFO.

The report states: 'No artefacts of unknown or unexplained origin have been reported or handed to the UK authorities, despite thousands of UAP reports. There are no SIGINT, ELINT or radiation measurements and little useful video or still IMINT.'

The report concludes: 'There is no evidence that any UAP, seen in the UKADR [UK Air Defence Region], are incursions by air-objects of any intelligent (extra-terrestrial or foreign) origin, or that they represent any hostile intent.'

The report attributes unexplained residual sightings to 'Buoyant Plasma Formation,' hypothesises that plasma-generated electromagnetic fields can induce perceptual alterations in close-encounter witnesses, and states that cases were attributable to the 'close proximity of plasma related fields' which could 'adversely affect a vehicle or person.'

The Condign executive summary recommends further research into 'novel military applications' of the plasma phenomenon and states that 'the implications have already been briefed to the relevant MoD technology managers' (Executive Summary, pp. 11-12).

The report notes that scientists in the former Soviet Union 'have identified the close connection between the UFO Phenomena and Plasma technologies' and are 'pursuing related techniques for potential military purposes' (Executive Summary, pp. 9-10).

For two decades the MoD withheld sections of volume 2 stamped NATO Secret, including text and two images relating to 'Black and other aircraft as UAP events,' citing FOIA exemptions 24 (national security) and 27 (international relations).

In February 2026 the MoD rejected a fresh FOI request for those sections on the grounds that 'even from this distance in time, its disclosure could still provide adversaries with an insight into the developments of US/UK aircraft technology, compromising the military capabilities of US partners and our own Air Force assets'; four months later the same images and text were released with zero redactions to a different requester.

The material withheld for twenty years consisted of two speculative paragraphs on the rumoured US Aurora/Astra programme and on the TR-3A 'Black Manta,' the latter annotated in Figure 5 with a 60ft wingspan, 42ft length, the description 'covert survivable in weather strike/recce,' and two variants, one 'seen with sausage-shaped contrail (or smoke?)' and one 'probably/possibly with pulsating motor.'

The report included head-on silhouettes of the F-117 and B-2 with the observation that their fuselage shapes 'can be reported respectively as "saucer or arc/boomerang shaped" under certain silhouette and lighting conditions,' captioned 'These aircraft types are unfamiliar as they are rarely spotted in UK airspace.'

The report's operative recommendation is reported to have been that it should no longer be a requirement for DI55 to monitor UAP reports; the exact verbatim wording of the recommendations section needs to be checked against the released MoD text.

dossier.denialPosture: The report itself is the denial artifact: a dated, signed, government-authored statement that no UAP in UK airspace are of intelligent extra-terrestrial or foreign origin and that no unknown artefacts were ever handed to UK authorities. The MoD separately maintained for two decades, most recently in February 2026, that specific redacted sections could not be released without compromising US/UK aircraft technology — a national-security justification it abandoned four months later by releasing the same material in full.
connections: DI55 and the Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence are the UK structural analogues of the US UAPTF/AARO lineage; the MoD abolished its UFO desk in 2009, eleven years before the US stood up the UAP Task Force.

Ron Haddow, named by David Clarke as the commissioned author, is the single named individual in the UK program chain; his clearance level, tasking authority and reporting line are the natural next research target.
The redacted sections tie Condign directly to US black aerospace programs (Aurora/Astra, TR-3A Black Manta) and therefore to the US SAP architecture governed by 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDD 5205.07.
The plasma/perceptual-effects hypothesis is a direct precursor of later prosaic-explanation framings used by AARO, and of the directed-energy and neurological-effects threads elsewhere on the board.
David Clarke is both the FOIA requester and the publisher of the 2022 Calvine photograph, linking Condign to the 1990 Calvine diamond-craft case and to RAF Machrihanish.

The MoD's stated reason for withholding — protecting 'the military capabilities of US partners' — makes the UK file formally subordinate to US classification equities, i.e. a foreign government holding a US secret about UAP.
openQuestions: Who inside DI55 tasked Haddow, and under what standing requirement was DI55 collecting UAP reports in the first place?
Which 'relevant MoD technology managers' received the plasma briefing, and did any research programme follow?
Did any US agency review, coordinate on, or object to portions of the report before or after the 2006 release, and is there a US-side copy?
What is in volume 3, and does the surviving original three-volume copy the MoD rediscovered (per Clarke's 2023 'Lost and Found' post) differ from the 2006 release?
Does the Condign statement that no artefacts were ever handed to UK authorities extend to materials held by UK contractors or transferred to US custody, or only to direct handovers to the MoD?

l0.label: Sky Canada Project - Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada

dossier.whatItIs: A review conducted by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada into how public reports of unidentified aerial phenomena are handled by the Canadian federal government, published in June 2025 as a 59-page report titled 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada,' carrying a message signed by Chief Science Advisor Mona Nemer. It surveyed federal departments, national and local police, civil aviation, the Coast Guard, citizen-science organizations and international comparators, and issued fourteen recommendations across reporting and data oversight, communications, research, and international collaboration.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Sky Canada Project is the board's cleanest documentation of concealment-by-non-recording, and it was written by a government about itself. Its central finding is that no Canadian federal body holds the UAP file: the RCMP has no policy, no classification and therefore no statistics; Transport Canada logs UAP into an aviation-safety database as an incidental category and does not investigate absent a safety concern; the RCAF does not investigate outside a threat or distress context; the National Research Council stopped collecting in 1995 and shipped fifteen thousand pages to the archives. Where no organization is responsible for a category of event, the absence of evidence is manufactured rather than observed, and every subsequent official statement that there is nothing to report becomes structurally true and evidentially worthless. The report also documents a measurable narrowing: direct submission of UAP reports from Canadian federal departments to independent researcher Chris Rutkowski, running since 2000, 'decreased significantly' by 2020, precisely as the American record was reopening. And it establishes the historical pattern, because Canada ran two named federal UAP programs, Project Magnet and Project Second Storey, and closed both on a committee finding that UFOs 'neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest,' the Canadian twin of the Robertson Panel logic. Finally, it is an ally-government artifact that treats AARO as a model and recommends formal partnership with it, showing how the American framing is exported into allied policy.
dossier.narrative:
Canada's federal engagement with the phenomenon is older than most assume and was twice institutionalized and twice shut down. In 1950 the Department of Transport granted engineer Wilbert Smith permission to research whether some UFOs might use the power of the Earth's magnetic field as a source of propulsion. That was Project Magnet. Smith expanded its scope to include validating UFO observations, launched a balloon over Ottawa to monitor public and media reaction, and established a UFO observatory outside the capital. The department terminated Project Magnet in 1954 and Smith continued privately. In 1952 the Defence Research Board established Project Second Storey, chaired by National Research Council astronomer Dr. Peter Millman with members from Canadian military intelligence and other agencies. Second Storey did not investigate sightings. It produced a reporting form that was never broadly adopted, met six times between 1952 and 1954, concluded that 'UFOs neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest,' and recommended ending all investigations by the Canadian military. That recommendation held for seventy years.

From 1954 to 1967 reports drifted to the RCMP, Transport Canada, National Defence and local police, occasionally logged, never systematized. In 1967, on the recommendation of the Minister of National Defence, the file went to the National Research Council, a transfer that included declassification of both Second Storey and Magnet. Millman personally answered public queries, usually with stars, planets, meteors and optical phenomena. In 1995 the NRC stopped collecting altogether and everything went to Library and Archives Canada, where the collection sits today at an estimated fifteen thousand pages, of which some nine thousand five hundred have been digitized. Over the last decade the NRC has processed only about forty UAP-related inquiries.

That is the vacuum the Sky Canada Project stepped into, and its consultations produced admissions more useful than any sighting. The RCMP, which serves roughly seventy-three percent of Canada's landmass and holds a federal investigative mandate nationwide, told the OCSA it has no formal policy for collection or dissemination of UAP reports and no classification system specific to UAPs, and that such reports are typically categorized as non-offence incidents under 'Aeronautics Act - Other Activities,' a bucket that also holds drone sightings. There is no guidance for call takers; a UAP call can be logged as a 'suspicious vehicle' and lost. The report states the consequence in a single sentence: 'It was therefore impossible for the RCMP to provide statistics about UAP reports.' The RCMP nonetheless told the OCSA it saw potential value in a dedicated office to which UAP reports could be referred.

Civil aviation is barely better. Transport Canada maintains the Civil Aviation Daily Occurrence Reporting System, into which NAV CANADA feeds roughly eighty percent of the content, and UAP sightings land in a category labelled 'Weather Balloon, Meteor, Rocket, UFO and Intelligence Sighting.' The report cites CTVNews.ca's January 2024 review of CADORS identifying only seventeen 2023 events that could be considered UAP, about 0.08 percent of pilot-reported incidences, and states the consequence directly: 'They are so rare in CADORS that Transport Canada is not incentivized to dedicate time and effort to explaining them. In fact, when such incidents do not raise serious safety concerns, Canadian authorities do not investigate further.' The RCAF 'does not typically investigate sightings of unexplained phenomena outside the context of investigating potential threats or distress.' The Coast Guard has a procedure, Vital Intelligence Sightings handled as MERINT reports, and used it twice between 2010 and 2022.

The report is also candid about why the scientific community stays away. It cites a survey of 1,460 tenured and tenure-track faculty at 144 research-intensive U.S. universities in which 53 percent believed UAP-related research would jeopardize their tenure or promotion, while only 7 percent held a negative opinion of such research. That gap is the mechanics of stigma quantified, and it is the same mechanism ODNI described in 2021.

Into the gap stepped civilians. Chris Rutkowski, co-founder of Ufology Research, began investigating in 1975 and has published the annual Canadian UFO Survey since 1989. From 2000 he began receiving reports directly from federal agencies including DND and Transport Canada. By 2020, the report records, 'the direct submission of UFO reports from federal departments decreased significantly,' and Ufology Research now relies primarily on public sources and access-to-information requests. A federal-to-civilian data channel that operated for twenty years quietly closed at the exact moment the topic reopened in Washington.

The fourteen recommendations are structured to rebuild the capacity Canada dismantled. Identify a federal lead, one that is 'a trusted and recognized scientific organization' with public communication capacity and an established international network: 'For example, the Canadian Space Agency could be considered for such a role.' Establish a dedicated service that collects testimonies, investigates cases and posts analyses publicly. Have Transport Canada encourage pilots, cabin crews and air traffic controllers to report without fear of stigmatization. Support public dialogue, mandate intra-governmental collaboration by internal directive, improve media relations, convene an expert panel on countering misinformation, facilitate open data, conduct periodic surveys, and support citizen science. And, internationally, 'establish partnerships with international entities dedicated to UAPs, such as AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile).'

That last recommendation is where the board should slow down. The report holds up AARO, established in 2022, as a structured, transparent model, alongside NASA's September 2023 study, France's GEIPAN inside CNES since 1977, and Chile's SEFAA. Canada is being advised to plug into the American architecture at the moment that architecture is under sustained challenge from congressional witnesses who characterize AARO as a barrier rather than a bridge. If Canada builds a UAP office whose primary international relationship is with AARO, then whatever AARO does not share, Canada will not have, and Canadian access-to-information law will not reach it. During the project the OCSA received about 250 inquiries from Canadians, including requests for help interpreting photos and videos, despite the website stating it offered no such service. That is an unanswered demand signal no Canadian institution is positioned to meet.

claims.text: The report 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada' was published by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada in June 2025, runs 59 pages, offers fourteen recommendations grouped under Reporting and Data Oversight, Communications, Research and International Collaboration, and carries a message signed by Chief Science Advisor Mona Nemer.

The report states that the RCMP 'does not have a formal policy for the collection or dissemination of UAP reports,' that 'there is no classification system specific to UAPs,' that such reports are typically categorized as non-offence incidents under 'Aeronautics Act - Other Activities,' and that consequently 'It was therefore impossible for the RCMP to provide statistics about UAP reports.'

The report states that the RCMP acknowledged during consultations the growing public interest in UAPs and 'the potential value of a dedicated office responsible for providing factual information and serving as a centralized body to which UAP reports could be referred,' so the RCMP could remain focused on criminal investigations and threats to public safety.

The report cites a January 2024 CTVNews.ca review of Transport Canada's CADORS database identifying only 17 events reported by pilots in 2023 that could be considered UAP, about 0.08 percent of all incidences reported by pilots, and states that 'when such incidents do not raise serious safety concerns, Canadian authorities do not investigate further.'
The report states that the Royal Canadian Air Force 'does not typically investigate sightings of unexplained phenomena outside the context of investigating potential threats or distress.'

The report states that the Canadian Coast Guard handles unidentified waterborne objects under 'Vital Intelligence Sightings' procedures as MERINT reports transmitted to the nearest Canadian or U.S. coast guard station, and that from 2010 to 2022 only two MERINT reports were filed, both to the CCG's Western region.

In 1950 the Department of Transport granted engineer Wilbert Smith permission to research whether some UFOs could use the power of the Earth's magnetic field as a source of propulsion, a project called Project Magnet, which Smith expanded to include investigating the validity of UFO observations and which the Department of Transport terminated in 1954.

In 1952 the Defence Research Board established Project Second Storey, a committee chaired by NRC astronomer Dr. Peter Millman with members from Canadian military intelligence and other agencies; it held six meetings from 1952 to 1954, concluded that 'UFOs neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest,' and recommended ending all investigations by the Canadian military.

In 1967 responsibility for UFO reports transferred to the National Research Council, including declassification of Project Second Storey and Project Magnet; the NRC stopped collecting UFO reports in 1995 and all related material was transferred to Library and Archives Canada, where the collection is estimated at 15,000 pages, of which some 9,500 have been digitized.

The NRC has processed about 40 UAP-related inquiries over the last decade, referring them to other government departments such as Transport Canada and Library and Archives Canada, as well as to local astronomy clubs.

Recommendation 1 states that a federal lead should be identified, that it should be 'a trusted and recognized scientific organization' with public communication capacity and an established international scientific network, and that 'For example, the Canadian Space Agency could be considered for such a role'; Recommendation 13 states that the lead organization 'should establish partnerships with international entities dedicated to UAPs, such as AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile).'

The report records that independent researcher Chris Rutkowski of Ufology Research began receiving UFO reports directly from federal agencies such as DND and Transport Canada starting in 2000, but that 'by 2020, the direct submission of UFO reports from federal departments decreased significantly,' leaving Ufology Research reliant primarily on publicly available sources and formal access to information requests.

The report cites a survey of 1,460 tenured and tenure-track faculty members at 144 research-intensive universities in the United States in which 53 percent believed UAP-related research would jeopardize their tenure or promotion, even though only 7 percent had a negative opinion of this type of research.

During the Sky Canada Project the Office of the Chief Science Advisor received about 250 inquiries from Canadians, including inquiries about where to report UAP sightings and requests for government assistance to interpret photos and videos, despite the project website stating the Office offered no such service.

The report's international comparison presents the U.S. Department of Defense's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (established 2022), NASA's September 2023 independent study and subsequent Director of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Research position, France's GEIPAN (operating under CNES since 1977), and Chile's SEFAA (within the General Directorate of Civil Aeronautics) as examples of coordinated, transparent and scientifically driven approaches to UAP reporting.

The report states that further follow-up on CADORS records may be undertaken by Transport Canada, NAV CANADA, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada, and the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), placing NORAD in the Canadian civil UAP reporting chain.

Next research step: determine whether the Government of Canada has formally responded to any of the fourteen recommendations, whether a lead department has been designated, and whether the Canadian Space Agency has accepted or declined the role.
claims.source: No Government of Canada response to the June 2025 report located in this research pass; status to be confirmed against ISED and CSA publications and Order Paper questions

dossier.denialPosture: Canada's operative denial is structural rather than rhetorical. The 1952-1954 Project Second Storey committee concluded that UFOs 'neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest' and recommended ending all military investigation, and that finding has never been formally revisited. Present-day departments do not deny the phenomenon; they decline to record it, with the RCMP unable to produce any statistics at all and Transport Canada explicitly not investigating absent a serious safety concern.
connections: Mona Nemer, Chief Science Advisor of Canada, is the signing official; the OCSA sits within Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada and is the only federal body to have examined the file since the NRC stopped collecting in 1995.

Wilbert Smith of the Department of Transport, who ran Project Magnet from 1950 to 1954, is the direct link into the American record and the Library and Archives Canada holdings on Magnet and Second Storey are the documentary starting point.

Dr. Peter Millman, NRC astronomer, chaired Project Second Storey and later personally answered public UFO queries for the NRC - one individual bridging the military closure of 1954 and the civil intake regime that ran to 1995.

CFS Falconbridge, Ontario is the Canadian node in the October-November 1975 SAC overflight wave (sac-overflights-1975); NORAD is named in this report as a possible follow-up body on CADORS records, meaning the same binational channel is still live fifty years later.

Recommendation 13's proposed partnership with AARO makes this report a vector by which the U.S. framing (odni-preliminary-assessment-2021 and its successor architecture) is institutionalized in allied policy and placed beyond Canadian access-to-information reach.

Chris Rutkowski and Ufology Research hold the only continuous Canadian dataset, the annual Canadian UFO Survey published since 1989; the documented post-2020 drying-up of federal submissions to him is a dated concealment event.

GEIPAN inside CNES since 1977 is the working counterexample: a national space agency openly holding the UAP file with a public archive, which is exactly what Recommendation 1 proposes for the Canadian Space Agency.

Matthew Hayes, 'Search for the Unknown: Canada's UFO Files and the Rise of Conspiracy Theory' (2022), and Chris Rutkowski, 'Canada's UFOs: Declassified' (2022), are the two named secondary works mining the LAC collection.
The report's faculty-survey finding on tenure risk quantifies the same stigma mechanism ODNI described in the 2021 assessment, giving the board a numeric handle on academic suppression.
openQuestions: Has the Government of Canada acted on any of the fourteen recommendations, and has a lead department been designated?
Why did direct submission of UAP reports from DND and Transport Canada to Ufology Research decrease significantly around 2020, was that a policy decision, and by whom?
What is in the roughly 5,500 pages of the Library and Archives Canada UFO collection that have not been digitized?
Does the Department of National Defence hold UAP-related operational reporting outside the public record, and was DND's holding examined or merely consulted during the Sky Canada Project?
Was the Project Second Storey finding of 1954 ever formally reviewed or rescinded, or does it remain the operative Canadian military position by default?
What did the OCSA's consultations with DND and the security services produce that did not make it into the published 59-page report?
How many of the 250 public inquiries to the OCSA involved imagery or physical evidence, and where was that material directed?
Does NORAD's binational structure mean Canadian UAP radar data is held on the U.S. side and therefore outside Canadian access-to-information reach?
Did Wilbert Smith's Project Magnet correspondence with U.S. counterparts survive in the LAC collection, and does it corroborate his claims about a classified American study?

l0.label: Immaculate Constellation disclosure, October-November 2024

dossier.whatItIs: Immaculate Constellation is the name of an alleged unacknowledged special access program that entered public reporting in October 2024 through the journalist Michael Shellenberger and entered the Congressional Record on 13 November 2024. According to the whistleblower report Shellenberger delivered to the House Oversight Committee, it was created by the Department of Defense in 2017 after the New York Times published on AATIP, and functions as a central or parent USAP consolidating UAP observations from tasked and untasked collection platforms. The Department of Defense has stated it has no record of any such program.
dossier.whyImplicated: The allegation is not that a secret exists but that a specific legal mechanism was used to keep it from Congress. Shellenberger's sworn written testimony states that a source told him the SAP 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code', adding: 'It is essentially a DOD Program, as the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.' The same testimony identifies the statutes that should have compelled notification - 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3093 - and asserts that the White House has a loophole for non-covert-action waived programs. That is a falsifiable structural claim about how a compartment can be run without triggering either SAP notification to the congressional defense committees or covert action findings to the intelligence committees. If true, it explains the entire pattern of this board: programmes that no oversight body can locate because no oversight body was ever the notification recipient.
dossier.narrative:
In October 2024 Michael Shellenberger, founder of the outlet Public, reported that a current or former US government official acting as a UAP whistleblower had provided him a report naming an active and highly secretive Department of Defense unacknowledged special access program. On 13 November 2024 he appeared under oath before the House Oversight Committee and the twelve-page document was entered into the Congressional Record from the dais.

His written testimony sets out the constitutional frame before it names anything. It cites 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3093 - the SAP notification statute and the covert action statute - and states: 'DEPSECDEF must notify congress regarding DOD SAPs and the President must notify regarding Covert Action. For UAPs this is apparently not happening because the White House has a loophole for non-covert action waived programs.' The whistleblower's own words, as quoted in the testimony, are that 'the Executive Branch has been managing UAP/NHI issues without Congressional knowledge, oversight, or authorization for some time, quite possibly decades.'

The source characterisation of the programme is that it 'is a "strategic intelligence program" that is part of the US military's family of long-standing, highly-sensitive programs dealing with various aspects of the UAP "problem."' The report itself, as quoted in the testimony, says 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION serves as a central or "parent" USAP that consolidates observations' of UAPs 'by both tasked and untasked collection platforms.' It 'includes high-quality Imagery Intelligence (IMINT) and Measurement and Signature Intelligence (MASINT) of UAPs', drawn from 'a blend of directed and incidental collection capabilities positioned in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the upper atmosphere' and at aviation and maritime altitudes. The most common shapes in the dataset are given as 'spheres/orbs, discs/saucers, ovals/tic-tacs, triangles, boomerang/arrowhead, and irregular/organic.'

The incident material is specific enough to be checkable by anyone with access to the underlying databases. One case: orbs surrounding and forcing an F-22 out of its patrol area, in which 'The F-22 broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs', with one UAP maintaining 'a rigid spatial relationship with the F-22, maintaining its exact position and orientation parallel with the F-22's cockpit despite multiple evasive rolls and maneuvers.' Another: the crew of a Navy aircraft carrier watching a 'small orange-red sphere' rapidly descend from high altitude to 100-200 yards directly above the flight deck. A third, sourced after publication: a roughly thirteen-minute high-definition full-colour video of a white orb emerging from the ocean approximately twenty miles off the coast of Kuwait, filmed from a helicopter, joined mid-video by a second orb, discovered by the source on SIPR.

The testimony also records a warning about the name itself. 'A source warned that simply printing the name "Immaculate Constellation" could trigger government surveillance of me under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of whoever publishes it. "They won't comment on it, but talking about it will put you in the danger zone," I was told.' From the dais that day Rep. Nancy Mace said the same thing out loud: 'And Representative Luna just told me, if I say, "Immaculate Constellation," I will be on some list. Maybe a FISA warrant. So, come at me bro, I guess.'

The Department's response is a records assertion, and Shellenberger printed it in his own testimony: 'DOD spokesperson Sue Gough said, "The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION.'"' That is not a statement that the programme does not exist. It is a statement about what a records search returned, made by a public affairs office that would not hold the read-on to an unacknowledged compartment. Mace's framing on the dais captured the structure exactly: '12 pages about this unacknowledged special access program that your government says does not exist.'

Two further items from the same hearing bear on the plausibility of the mechanism rather than the name. Retired Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, formerly the Navy's chief meteorologist, testified: 'I concluded that the UAP information must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency. That is, a compartmented program that even senior officials, including myself, were not read into.' And Luis Elizondo, asked directly by Mace whether he was read into secret UAP crash retrieval programmes, answered: 'We would have to have a conversation in a closed session, ma'am. I signed documentation 3 years ago that restricts my ability to discuss specifically crash retrievals.'

Under questioning from Rep. Clay Higgins, Shellenberger confirmed he knows the report's author - 'I do' - and declined to characterise the author's institutional position. Asked by Mace what the programme's mission is, he answered that it is an unacknowledged special access program whose 'mission is to document UAPs'. He also stated that when he checked the report against existing public cases he 'did not find it based on existing cases; it was new cases for me', which he offered as evidence against circular reporting.

What the record does not contain is any independent corroboration of the name from a second identified source, any document bearing the programme name, or any executive branch statement beyond the records denial. The name has never appeared in an AARO annual report, in any PURSUE tranche description, or in any published DoD product.
dossier.denialPosture: Department of Defense spokesperson Sue Gough is quoted in Shellenberger's written testimony as saying: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION."' That is a records assertion rather than a denial of existence, and it is the standard formulation available to an office without read-on to an unacknowledged compartment. Rep. Mace characterised it from the dais as a programme 'that your government says does not exist'. No further departmental statement has been made in the twenty-one months since.
openQuestions: The identity and institutional position of the report's author, which Shellenberger confirmed he knows but declined to disclose.
Whether any congressional committee has formally requested a SAP notification search under 10 U.S.C. 119 against the alleged programme, and what the response was.
Whether the 'non-covert action waived program' loophole described in the testimony is a real category in current SAP practice, and which office administers such programmes.

Whether the specific incidents described - the F-22 boxing event, the CVN flight deck sphere, the Kuwait helicopter video on SIPR - correspond to identifiable case numbers in AARO, UAPTF or service databases.
No document bearing the programme name has ever been published; the only artefact in the public record is the twelve-page report entered by Rep. Mace.
Claims elsewhere that former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick denied the programme could not be verified against a primary source for this dossier and are not asserted here.

Maybe a FISA warrant. So, come at me bro, I guess.'
Asked by Rep. Mace what the programme's mission is and how it is funded, Shellenberger answered under oath: 'it is an unacknowledged special access program. Its mission is to document UAPs.'

l0.label: STAR GATE and predecessor remote viewing programs, 1970-1995
l0.short: STAR GATE and predecessor remote viewing programs, 1970-1995

dossier.whatItIs: STAR GATE was the final code name for a U.S. government psychic-intelligence effort that ran from roughly 1970 to 1995 under a rotating series of names and host agencies: SCANATE (CIA-funded, from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM Detachment G at Fort Meade, 1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, 1985), and STAR GATE (DIA with SAIC as prime contractor, 1991). It combined an operational collection unit that tasked trained remote viewers against real intelligence targets with a separately maintained contract research program run out of Stanford Research Institute. It was terminated in 1995 after a Congressionally Directed Action moved it to CIA and CIA declined to keep it.
dossier.whyImplicated: STAR GATE is the board's cleanest declassified proof-of-concept for the exact institutional pattern the legacy program is alleged to follow: a real, funded, operational, compartmented effort into a phenomenon the government publicly treated as nonsense, sustained across two decades and at least four host organizations by serial renaming, moved between Army, DIA and CIA in a way that defeats continuity of oversight, and run through a cleared contractor (SRI, then SAIC) rather than in-house. The 1995 CIA program-status memorandum shows the disposal mechanics with unusual clarity: CIA and DIA had already made 'plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' before any evaluation was complete, and the memo's author recommended asking Congress to agree the program should NOT transfer to CIA before the contracted review had even begun. That is a decision to terminate reached in advance of the evidence, followed by a curated declassification, which means the archive the public got is the residue of a deliberate sorting operation rather than a data dump. The program also demonstrates that a phenomenon-adjacent effort could be carried in the black for twenty-five years while officials denied its existence, and that its closure could be framed publicly as a scientific verdict rather than a bureaucratic one. Finally, STAR GATE is a personnel bridge: the scientists, contractors and case officers it credentialed are the same names that reappear in the NIDS, AAWSAP and To The Stars-era record, giving the board a documented lineage from Cold War compartmented research to the 2017-2026 disclosure fight.
dossier.narrative:
The origin story is threat-mirroring. Between 1969 and 1971, U.S. intelligence concluded the Soviet Union was investing seriously in what it called psychotronics, with estimates running to 60 million rubles per year by 1970 and over 300 million by 1975. Whether or not the Soviets had anything, the money itself was treated as evidence, and CIA opened a research line in 1970 under the name SCANATE. In 1972 the research moved to Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, where Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff ran it, initially around a small set of gifted individuals including the artist Ingo Swann. The client requirement, per the FAS program file, was a minimum accuracy of 65 percent.

The operational side grew separately out of the Army. GONDOLA WISH, a 1977 Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence effort under the Systems Exploitation Detachment, was chartered to evaluate potential adversary applications of remote viewing. It became a collection project in mid-1978 as GRILL FLAME, INSCOM 'Detachment G,' housed in buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, Maryland. The SRI research was folded into GRILL FLAME in early 1979, and hundreds of experiments were run at SRI through 1986. Renamed the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project in 1983, the unit adopted a written methodology developed by Swann and Puthoff meant to make the capability trainable rather than innate. Its existence surfaced publicly when columnist Jack Anderson reported on it in April 1984. That same year the National Academy of Sciences' National Research Council evaluated remote viewing for the Army Research Institute and returned an unfavorable verdict. When Army funding ended in late 1985, the unit did not die; it was redesignated SUN STREAK and moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate under office code DT-S. In 1991 the contract moved to Science Applications International Corporation and the program became STAR GATE, downgraded from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS, limited dissemination, program. Edwin May presided over roughly 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of data collection. Over two decades the effort consumed on the order of $20 million, with about $11 million spent from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, and involved more than forty personnel including about twenty-three remote viewers.

The end is where the concealment mechanics are legible. The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed transfer to CIA and directed CIA to conduct a retrospective review. What happened next is documented in a SECRET memorandum, 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction,' now in the CIA reading room as CIA-RDP96-00791R000100160001-0. The Executive Director approved CIA's approach in late January 1995; it was transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the Senate Appropriations Committee staff on 27 March 1995. CIA transferred funds to the Army Research Institute to make it executive agent for a National Research Council blue-ribbon review. In parallel, and this is the sentence that matters for the board, CIA was 'working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate' and had 'made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program.' The sorting of what the public would eventually see was underway before the verdict was in.

NRC declined the review by letter dated 5 May 1995, citing its own 1988 report and quoting its conclusion that the case for remote viewing was 'not just very weak, but virtually nonexistent.' NRC referred CIA to Dr. David Goslin, president of the American Institutes for Research. The memo's author then recommended skipping the review entirely: 'in view of the strong position taken by the NRC... I want to propose at this point that we strongly consider the option of going back to Congress with the recommendation not to accept the Star Gate program from DIA,' adding that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.' He also recorded that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and deferred any decision about the operational personnel still at DIA. The recommendation was explicit: 'ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA.'

AIR did the review anyway. Its final report is dated 29 September 1995 and was released publicly on 28 November 1995. It contained two irreconcilable assessments, statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect and psychologist Ray Hyman finding none, and a single recommendation to terminate. CIA's public line was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations. The program had been sustained politically for years by Senator Claiborne Pell of Rhode Island and Representative Charles Rose of North Carolina; with the program dead, the constituency dissolved.

What the board should take from STAR GATE is not whether remote viewing worked. It is the demonstrated administrative repertoire: serial renaming across host commands, movement between Army, DIA and CIA, SAP-to-LIMDIS reclassification, contractor intermediation, a pre-cooked termination decision, a curated declassification, and a public verdict framed in the language of science rather than of budget politics. Every one of those moves is available to any program that wants to disappear while remaining funded, and every one is documented here in the government's own paper.

claims.text: A SECRET CIA memorandum titled 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction' records that a Congressionally Directed Action transferred the STAR GATE program to CIA, that the Executive Director approved CIA's recommended approach in late January 1995, and that the approach was 'formally transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the SAC staff on 27 March 1995.'

The same CIA memorandum states that CIA 'have been working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate and have made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' - meaning the scope of the eventual public release was decided before the outside evaluation was performed.

The same CIA memorandum records that the National Research Council declined to perform the evaluation by letter dated 5 May 1995, and that CIA was then referred to Dr. David Goslin, President of the American Institutes for Research.

The same CIA memorandum recommends terminating before the review is performed: 'I recommend we adopt this alternative plan and ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA,' noting that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.'

The same CIA memorandum states that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and that a decision on the operational personnel then at DIA was deferred pending the blue-ribbon panel assessment.

The American Institutes for Research final report, 'An Evaluation of Remote Viewing: Research and Applications,' is dated 29 September 1995 and was released to the public on 28 November 1995; its final recommendation was to terminate the STAR GATE effort.

STAR GATE was the last in a chain of renamed programs: SCANATE (CIA-funded from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI Systems Exploitation Detachment, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM 'Detachment G,' buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, mid-1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE Project (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, late 1985), STAR GATE (1991).

In 1991 the program transitioned to Science Applications International Corporation (SAIC) and was changed from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS (limited dissemination) program; Edwin May presided over 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of the program's data collection.

Remote viewing research began in 1972 at Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California, conducted by Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff, initially focused on a small number of individuals including Ingo Swann.

Over more than two decades roughly $20 million was spent on STAR GATE and related activities, with about $11 million budgeted from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s; over forty personnel served in the program at various times, including about twenty-three remote viewers.
The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed that the program be transferred to CIA and that CIA conduct a retrospective review of it.
The program's political survival depended on two named legislators: Senator Claiborne Pell (D-RI) and Representative Charles Rose (D-NC).

The existence of the then-highly-classified program was publicly reported by columnist Jack Anderson in April 1984; a 1984 National Academy of Sciences / National Research Council evaluation performed for the Army Research Institute returned unfavorable results.

The AIR evaluation contained a positive assessment by statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect, offset by a negative assessment by psychologist Ray Hyman; CIA's public conclusion was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations.

Next research step: establish the exact volume and cut-off criteria of the STAR GATE material released into CIA's electronic reading room through the January 2017 CREST expansion, and identify what categories of record are absent from it, against the 1995 decision to withhold 'the most sensitive aspects of the program.'
claims.source: CIA electronic reading room, STAR GATE records (example record: https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/document/cia-rdp96-00791r000100160001-0); collection-level page count not verified against a CIA-published figure

dossier.denialPosture: CIA's public position at termination was that remote viewing had never produced data used to guide an intelligence operation and that the program was scientifically unsupported, a verdict delivered through a contracted outside evaluator rather than in CIA's own voice. The 1995 internal memorandum shows that position was arrived at before the evaluation was contracted, and that the declassification package was scoped in parallel by CIA and DIA to exclude 'the most sensitive aspects of the program.'
connections: Harold Puthoff and Russell Targ ran the SRI research leg under CIA and later DIA sponsorship; Puthoff is a recurring node in the modern UAP-contracting record (NIDS, AAWSAP-era work, To The Stars Academy). His exact TTSA officer title and dates should be confirmed against SEC filings for CIK 0001710274.

SAIC as STAR GATE prime contractor from 1991 to 1995 places the program inside the same cleared-contractor ecosystem as later phenomenon-adjacent work; SAIC's successor entities are standing nodes for the funding thread.

DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate (DT-S) hosted the program from 1985 to 1991; DIA is the same agency that later hosted AAWSAP, making DIA the most persistent institutional host across both threads.
Richard D'Amato, Senate Appropriations Committee staff, is the named congressional staff recipient of the 27 March 1995 CIA briefing, a specific and findable oversight contact point.
Army INSCOM at Fort Meade is the operational home; INSCOM connects to the Army-side custody question raised by the TTSA-Army CRADA (ttsa-army-crada) four decades later.

The pattern of serial renaming and inter-agency transfer is the template the board applies to the alleged legacy recovery program; STAR GATE is the control case where the template is documented rather than inferred.

American Institutes for Research and its president David Goslin are the named third-party validators used to close the program, the same 'independent review' device later used with the NASA 2023 UAP study panel and AARO's Historical Record Report.

l0.label: UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports I-VII (Stringfield, 1978-1994)

dossier.whatItIs: The Status Reports are a series of seven self-published monographs by Cincinnati ufologist Leonard H. Stringfield (1920-1994), issued between 1978 and 1994, compiling anonymized first- and second-hand accounts of alleged U.S. military recoveries of crashed craft and occupant bodies. The first, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody,' was presented at the Ninth Annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio in July 1978. The series is the foundational corpus of the modern crash-retrieval literature.
dossier.whyImplicated: Every modern claim about a legacy retrieval program is downstream of a source pool that Stringfield assembled first. His method — solicit military and medical personnel, strip identities, publish coded case abstracts — created a body of testimony in the late 1970s and 1980s whose content is structurally identical to what witnesses told the House Oversight Committee in 2023 and 2024: recovery of intact and damaged craft, transport to secure facilities, autopsy of non-human remains, compartmented handling outside normal channels. If those 2023 claims are a modern fabrication, the fabrication is forty-five years old and was published in monograph form by a MUFON public relations director with a documented Air Defense Command reporting relationship. If they are not, Stringfield's files are the earliest systematic index of the program's personnel. Either way, the corpus is a testable object: the sources are anonymous, but the cases carry dates, units and installations, and the underlying files exist as a physical archive. The honest tier here is low on the substance and high on the provenance.
dossier.narrative:
Stringfield's standing rests on a career that predates the crash-retrieval work by two decades. In 1954 he founded Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects (CRIFO) in Cincinnati and published the newsletter ORBIT. He wrote 'Inside Saucer Post...3-0 Blue: CRIFO Views the Status Quo' in 1957, the same year he became public relations adviser to Donald Keyhoe's National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena. From 1967 to 1969 he served as an 'Early Warning Coordinator' for the Condon Committee at the University of Colorado, screening incoming reports for possible scientific study. He was later Director of Public Relations for the Mutual UFO Network. His day job, throughout, was Director of Public Relations and Marketing Services for DuBois Chemicals, a division of Chemed Corporation. He died of lung cancer on 18 December 1994.

The relevant biographical detail for a concealment analysis is the reporting arrangement. NICAP's own biography states that Stringfield worked in cooperation with the U.S. Air Force from 1953 to 1957 investigating and reporting UFO activity, having been assigned a special code number for reporting to the Air Defense Command in Columbus, Ohio. A civilian researcher holding an assigned reporting code to ADC is an unusual artifact and it explains why military personnel later approached him rather than a journalist.

The Status Report series, with titles and dates as published: Status Report I, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A case study of alleged UFOs and occupants in military custody' (1978, from the Ninth Annual MUFON Symposium, Dayton, Ohio, July 1978); Status Report II, 'The UFO Crash/Retrieval Syndrome: New Sources, New Data' (1980); Status Report III, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Amassing the Evidence' (1982); Status Report IV, 'The fatal encounter at Ft. Dix-McGuire: A case study' (1985); Status Report V, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Is the coverup lid lifting?' (1989); Status Report VI, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: The Inner Sanctum' (1991); Status Report VII, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Search for Proof in a Hall of Mirrors' (1994). All were self-published. A 2019 compilation reissued all seven in one volume.

The method is the weakness and also the reason the corpus is worth auditing. Stringfield presented cases as numbered abstracts summarizing accounts from unnamed informants, most described as military or medical personnel. Some abstracts are explicitly composites; the widely cited 'Abstract XXII: Biological data relating to retrieved alien bodies' is described as a composite assembled from anonymous medical and military sources. No abstract in the published series can be independently verified from the text alone, because the text withholds the identifying information that would permit verification. That is a disqualifying defect for any individual claim and simultaneously the exact behavior one would expect from a researcher protecting serving personnel.

Status Report IV is the outlier and the best single entry point for an analyst. It abandons the abstract format for a single named case study, the alleged January 1978 incident at Fort Dix and McGuire Air Force Base in New Jersey, with a specific installation, a specific date window, and identifiable military police and security police units. That case is checkable against Army and Air Force records in a way the composite abstracts are not.

The physical archive survives. MUFON's Project Aquarius Library lists the Stringfield Files as a private collection. The underlying correspondence, informant notes and case files in that collection are the actual evidentiary object; the published monographs are only the redacted output. Whether the collection contains unredacted informant identities is the single most consequential unanswered question about this entity.

What the record shows: a well-documented researcher with an unusual official reporting relationship who, over sixteen years, published seven monographs compiling anonymous military testimony about recoveries and autopsies, and who left an archive. What the record does not show: any named source, any document, any physical item, or any independent corroboration of a single abstract. Tiered honestly, the existence, authorship, dating and archival survival of the Status Reports are Tier 1 or 2; every substantive claim inside them is Tier 3 pending identification of sources.

dossier.denialPosture: No U.S. government body has ever formally addressed the Stringfield Status Reports by name. AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 does not engage the Stringfield corpus, though it broadly asserts that alleged reverse-engineering and recovery programs described to it either do not exist or are misidentifications of authentic sensitive programs. The silence is itself notable given that the reports are the origin point for much of the claim structure AARO was chartered to resolve.
connections: Stringfield's Air Defense Command reporting code (Columbus, Ohio, 1953-1957) places him inside the early USAF civilian-reporting apparatus alongside Project Blue Book-era filtering, making him a bridge between official 1950s reporting channels and the private crash-retrieval literature.
His Condon Committee 'Early Warning Coordinator' role from 1967-1969 links him to the last official U.S. scientific study of UFOs before the subject was formally dropped by the Air Force.
MUFON is both the venue for Status Report I and the current custodian of the Stringfield Files, making it the single institution holding the unredacted source material.
The Fort Dix-McGuire case in Status Report IV is the only installation-and-date-specific claim in the series and is the natural target for FOIA against Army and Air Force security police records.

The structural content of Stringfield's abstracts — recovery, transport, secure facility, autopsy of non-human remains, compartmented handling — is the same claim structure David Grusch presented to the House Oversight Committee in 2023 and that AARO attributes to KONA BLUE-derived misinterpretation.
Donald Keyhoe and NICAP connect Stringfield to the 1950s-60s civilian pressure campaign for congressional hearings, the direct ancestor of the 2023-2025 Oversight hearings.
Eric Gairy's 1978 UN initiative gives Stringfield a documented, if brief, foreign-government advisory role in the same year as Status Report I.
openQuestions: Do the Stringfield Files at MUFON contain unredacted informant identities, and under what access conditions?
Was the special ADC reporting code assigned to Stringfield an official Air Force arrangement, and does a USAF record of it exist?
One catalog record dates 'Retrievals of the Third Kind' to 5 April 1978 while the symposium was held in July 1978; which is the paper's actual first distribution date?
Are any of Stringfield's abstracts traceable to individuals who later surfaced in the AATIP, KONA BLUE or AARO interview pools?
Do Army or Air Force records substantiate any incident at Fort Dix-McGuire in the January 1978 window described in Status Report IV?
Did Stringfield ever provide his files or informant identities to any federal entity, and was he ever contacted by one?
How much of the corpus is independent testimony versus recirculation of a small number of original informants? No source-mapping of the seven reports has been published.

l0.label: The Roswell Report: Case Closed (1997)

dossier.whatItIs: The Roswell Report: Case Closed is a 231-page official United States Air Force publication authored by Capt. James McAndrew of the Secretary of the Air Force Declassification and Review Team at the Pentagon, printed by the U.S. Government Printing Office and released on 24 June 1997. It is the follow-on to the 1994-95 Air Force report The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert by Col. Richard L. Weaver and then-1st Lt. James McAndrew. Its purpose is to account for the reports of 'alien bodies' that the 1995 report had left unaddressed.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is a denial artifact, and it is catalogued here as evidence about the denier rather than about Roswell. It is dated, signed, congressionally provoked, and printed at government expense, which makes it the most attributable statement the Air Force has ever made on the subject - and its internal logic reveals precisely which claims the Air Force judged it could not leave standing. Its core mechanism is temporal: it asserts that Air Force activities spread across many years have been consolidated by witnesses into two or three days in July 1947, and that UFO proponents mis-dated the 'alien' observations "in some instances by more than a decade." It was released on the 50th anniversary of the Kenneth Arnold sighting, a date choice that is itself a communications decision. And it is the direct product of a General Accounting Office audit initiated at the request of a sitting member of Congress, which means the Air Force wrote it under external compulsion rather than voluntarily - the only such instance in the pre-2017 record. The GAO audit that produced it also established, on the record, that Roswell Army Air Field's administrative records for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing messages for October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, with no indication of by whom or under what authority.
dossier.narrative:
The sequence matters more than the content. In 1993 Rep. Steven H. Schiff (R-New Mexico) began asking the Department of Defense about Roswell and, dissatisfied, referred the matter to the General Accounting Office. The GAO tasking forced the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force into an exhaustive records search that concluded in July 1994 and produced roughly 1,000 pages of material, published in 1995 as The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert. Secretary of the Air Force Sheila E. Widnall released interviewees from any security obligations that might have restricted their statements. The 1995 report's answer was Project Mogul: a then-classified balloon-borne acoustic sensor program whose train components, it said, accounted for the debris. Notably, the Mogul records that carried the explanatory weight had never been classified at all; other Mogul records had been declassified en masse under Executive Order 11652, signed by President Nixon on 6 March 1972.

Mogul explained debris. It did not explain bodies. Case Closed exists to close that gap, and its four stated conclusions are worth reading as a list of the specific narrative threads the Air Force needed cut. First, that Air Force activities occurring over a period of many years "have been consolidated and are now represented to have occurred in two or three days in July 1947." Second, that "'Aliens' observed in the New Mexico desert were probably anthropomorphic test dummies that were carried aloft by U.S. Air Force high altitude balloons for scientific research." Third, that the reports of military units arriving shortly after a crash to retrieve a saucer and its crew "were actually accurate descriptions of Air Force personnel engaged in anthropomorphic dummy recovery operations." Fourth, that claims of bodies at the Roswell Army Air Field hospital were most likely a conflation of a 1956 KC-97 accident in which eleven airmen were killed and a 1959 manned balloon mishap in which two pilots were injured.

Read as an intelligence product, this is a substitution table. Each item on the left is a witness-reported element of a retrieval operation - non-human bodies, a cordon, a convoy, a hospital, injured or dead personnel - and each item on the right is a real, documented, unclassified Air Force activity that produces the same observable. The Air Force is not arguing that nothing happened. It is arguing that everything happened, repeatedly, over fifteen years, and that the witnesses stacked it. The named substitutes are Projects High Dive and Excelsior, the Holloman-based dummy-drop and high-altitude-bailout programs; the dummies are identified in the report's own figures as Alderson Laboratories and 'Sierra Sam' type anthropomorphic dummies. Appendix B is a set of signed sworn statements from in-person interviews, including Col. Charles A. Coltman Jr. (USAF Medical Corps, retired), Col. Dan D. Fulgham (retired) - the pilot injured in the 1959 balloon mishap - and Bernard D. Gildenberg, the Holloman balloon engineer.

The report's own framing gives away its function. It states that its findings run "Contrary to allegations that the Air Force has engaged in a cover-up and possesses dark secrets involving the Roswell claims." That sentence is not a finding; it is a rebuttal, and it identifies the audience. The title itself - Case Closed - is a declaration of jurisdiction over when an inquiry ends, which is the specific authority a service branch does not actually have with respect to Congress.

What the report does not address is the record-destruction finding that emerged from the same GAO audit. GAO/NSIAD-95-187, released 28 July 1995, reported that RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, and that the document disposition form did not indicate what organization or person destroyed them, when, or under what authority. The GAO also found that Army Air Force regulations in 1947 required air accident reports to be maintained permanently, that four such accidents were reported in New Mexico in July 1947 - all after 8 July, the date the RAAF public information office announced recovery of a flying disc - and that USAF officials told GAO there was no requirement to report the crash of a balloon.

Case Closed has since been absorbed into the current official narrative without qualification. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume 1, published 8 March 2024, cites it approvingly, restating the dummy explanation and the 1956/1959 hospital conflation verbatim as established results. That continuity is the point: the 1997 denial is not a historical curiosity, it is a live load-bearing element of the 2024 denial.

dossier.denialPosture: This document is the denial. It asserts finality in its title, expressly rejects "allegations that the Air Force has engaged in a cover-up," and explains every witness-reported element of a retrieval operation as a misdated observation of an unclassified Air Force program. It is a denial of interpretation rather than of events, which is a distinct and more durable rhetorical form.
